text: Jesús Alejandro Márquez Jiménez was the founder and editor of the news website Orión Informativo and a former reporter for the local newspaper Crítica in Tepic, Nayarit. According to the ONU-DH, his journalistic work focused on politics and current affairs. RSF reported that Orión Informativo had published criticism concerning alleged links between organised crime and local politicians in Nayarit, and that municipal officials in a neighbouring municipality had filed a defamation complaint against Márquez Jiménez approximately six months before his death.

Márquez Jiménez was last seen alive on 30 November 2018 after receiving a telephone call while eating with his family, whereupon he left his home on a motorcycle. His body was found the following morning — the day of President López Obrador’s inauguration — in a ditch near the Tepic airport. Anonymous sources cited by Crítica reported that the body bore at least four bullet wounds and signs of a beating.

FEADLE opened an investigation into the killing. ONU-DH called on authorities to conduct a prompt investigation, ensure those responsible are brought to justice, and emphasised the importance of ending impunity in cases of violence against journalists. The State Attorney General’s Office subsequently issued arrest warrants against three state government officials for the murder, including the Director General of Transit of Nayarit. The latter pleaded guilty to encubrimiento (cover-up), but two other Transit Department officials were charged as the alleged material authors of the killing and held in pretrial detention, but no conviction for Marquez’s kidnapping and murder has been recorded.

Rafael Murúa Manríquez was a community radio journalist and the founding director of Radio Kashana (93.3 FM), a community radio station affiliated with AMARC México in Santa Rosalía, Baja California Sur. He also collaborated with several other outlets, including Peninsular Digital, El Sur Californiano, BCS Noticias, and the Colectivo Pericú. He addressed cultural and political topics and was also recognised as a human rights defender and activist by the Organisation of American States.

Murúa had reported experiencing threats and harassment for several years prior to his killing. He was incorporated into Mexico’s federal Protection Mechanism in June 2017, after receiving threatening messages from an alleged member of a criminal gang. Despite being incorporated into the Mechanism, Murúa’s family noted that the home infrastructure measures and emergency button he was promised were never fully installed. Since November 2018, he had publicly denounced multiple incidents—including death threats, an attempted arbitrary detention, and a gunshot fired at his home—following reporting and opinions critical of Mulegé Mayor Felipe Prado Bautista’s administration. In a first-person account republished by Periodistas de a Pie, Murúa described a crowd pounding on his home’s gate, a bullet breaking an upstairs window, and a municipal police commander arriving at his newsroom seeking to detain him in circumstances he characterised as extrajudicial.

Murúa was reported missing on 19 January 2019 and his body was found the following day near an expressway approximately 40 kilometres north of Santa Rosalía. Forensic reports indicated that he suffered a stab wound that perforated the heart and left lung, as well as cranial trauma from a bullet impact. The State Attorney General’s Office announced that investigators found packages believed to contain marijuana at the scene—a fact condemned by ARTICLE 19 and AMARC México as an apparent attempt to blame the victim and deflect attention from the perpetrators.

On 27 January 2020, the State Attorney General’s Office announced that three suspects had been found guilty of carrying out Murúa’s murder and sentenced to 43 years and 9 months in prison. ARTICLE 19 and AMARC México continued to highlight alleged investigative shortcomings and the fundamental failure of the Mechanism to protect a journalist who was a registered beneficiary at the time of his murder. UNESCO’s Director-General also condemned the murder and emphasised the importance of protecting community media for freedom of expression and access to information.

Martín Valtierra García was the editor and founder of the news website Contrastes de Comondú, which covered news throughout Baja California Sur, including municipal payroll spending, nepotism within the municipal administration, and water shortages in several neighbourhoods. On 8 January 2019, he published a column critical of Comondú Mayor José Walter Valenzuela. Although he had not received direct threats, a colleague warned him in November 2018 that his reporting had angered officials in the municipal government. At the time of the attack, Valtierra was in the process of being incorporated into the federal Protection Mechanism.

On 29 January 2019, two unknown assailants attacked Valtierra with baseball bats outside his home in Ciudad Constitución. Security-camera footage confirmed by Valtierra showed two men exiting a vehicle, approaching him, striking him repeatedly, and then fleeing. He suffered a head wound requiring 12 stitches and a fractured right ulna, and was scheduled for surgery to repair the fracture.

Baja California Sur Governor Carlos Mendoza condemned the attack and promised that the state prosecutor’s office would open an investigation. In May 2019, authorities detained a suspect identified as Fidel “N,” described as a Comondú municipal government employee and the owner of the vehicle in which the attackers travelled. Valtierra subsequently died in an unrelated traffic collision on 21 January 2024.

Jesús Eugenio Ramos Rodríguez, known as “Chuchín,” was a veteran radio journalist who had worked for approximately 20 years at radio station Oye 99.9 FM in Emiliano Zapata, Tabasco, where he hosted the popular news programme Nuestra Región Hoy. According to his brother, the programme had become increasingly controversial in the wake of recent municipal elections, and Ramos Rodríguez had criticised local politicians on the programme.

On the morning of 9 February 2019, while Ramos Rodríguez was having breakfast at Hotel Ramos in Emiliano Zapata with several other individuals, a lone gunman entered the restaurant and shot him at close range. He died later that morning at the municipal hospital. The Tabasco State Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation and dispatched investigative and forensic personnel. The Tabasco prosecutor also requested that FEADLE join the investigation. ONU-DH called on authorities to investigate effectively, including the victim’s journalistic activity as a line of investigation, and to adopt effective protection measures for his family and colleagues. As of July 2019, RSF and CPJ reported that there had been no conviction in the case. In December 2020, a Tabasco police officer described as a presumed killer of Ramos Rodríguez was arrested, but for extortion, not for the journalist’s murder. To date, no conviction for the killing has been reported.

Reynaldo López Salas was a 51-year-old radio announcer, communications graduate of the Universidad de Sonora, and former sports presenter for Televisa Sonora. Carlos Andrés Cota Rubio was a sports journalist who had also worked at Televisa Sonora until the end of 2018, when he left to focus on a project called Motores del Desierto.

On the afternoon of 16 February 2019, López Salas and Cota Rubio were travelling together in a vehicle at the intersection of Bulevar Serna and Calle California in Hermosillo when an armed group in another car opened fire with AK-47 rifles in an attack lasting less than 40 seconds. López Salas was killed. Cota Rubio, who sustained 14 gunshot wounds, was transported to hospital in critical condition but ultimately survived. The CNDH condemned the attack and requested that state authorities provide medical attention and security to Cota Rubio and protective measures for the families.

The Sonora prosecutor’s office claimed that the attack was not related to the victims’ professional activity and suggested an alternative line of investigation related to alleged illegal activities of people close to one of the victims, a characterization that drew scrutiny from press freedom organisations. The OAS Special Rapporteur for Freedom of Expression included López among journalists killed in Mexico in its May 2019 press release condemning violence against journalists. In February 2024, three men—José Carlos “N”, Jorge Alberto “N”, and Adán Isaac “N”—were sentenced to 76 years and four months in prison for the homicide and attempted homicide.

On 20 February 2019, at approximately 5:30 a.m., Samir Flores Soberanes, an Indigenous Nahua community radio journalist and human rights defender, was shot and killed outside his home in Amilcingo in the state of Morelos. According to a joint statement issued by several CSOs, armed assailants arrived in two vehicles, knocked on his door, and shot him four times as he emerged, including two bullets to the head. He died shortly afterwards. Flores Soberanes was the co-founder and producer of Radio Amiltzinko (100.7 FM). His reporting and organising focused on environmental and Indigenous land-rights issues, including opposition to the Proyecto Integral Morelos, a federal energy megaproject comprising two thermoelectric plants in Huexca, an approximately 160-kilometre natural gas pipeline traversing the states of Tlaxcala, Puebla, and Morelos, an aqueduct drawing from the Cuautla River, and an electric transmission line; opponents argued the project would contaminate water supplies relied upon by Indigenous communities.

The killing occurred the morning after Flores Soberanes had attended a government-organised informational forum in Jonacatepec at which he publicly challenged the federal delegate Hugo Erik Flores Cervantes regarding the project, and three days before a federally scheduled public consultation on the project. According to the People's Front in Defence of Land and Water, Flores Soberanes had received repeated death threats in connection with his land-defence work since 2012, and had been subject to defamation and online harassment. Within hours of the killing, the Morelos State Attorney General, Uriel Carmona Gándara, publicly stated that the murder appeared linked to organised crime and asserted that there was no element connecting it to the thermoelectric project. A handwritten cardboard sign attributed to “Comando Tlahuica,” an organised crime group, was reportedly left at the scene of the killing, bearing a narcomanta or narcomensaje reading,  "X you fucking gossip, you reported [denounced] Abraham Ocampo and you keep on, you Michoacano with your fucking gang. Sincerely, Tlahuica Command.” The cardboard was lost by investigators in the course of the investigation. The lawyer for the Flores Soberanes family, together with the CNI, publicly stated that they did not trust the Morelos Attorney General's Office to conduct an impartial investigation, and called for the case to be transferred to federal jurisdiction. By late 2021, arrest warrants had been issued for three suspects. One, Azael Martínez, was dead at the time of issue; another, Salvador Aparicio, was missing; and the last, Javier Rosendo Pareja, was incarcerated at the time of the murder. Pareja was put on trial for Flores Soberante’s murder in February 2026, in a decision described by his neighbor and fellow activist Samantha Cesar as “a set-up.” He was acquitted in March 2026, after a trial rife with irregularities that included two of the prosecution’s key witnesses being killed and its evidence being found implausible or illegally obtained.  On 6 June 2026, alleged leader of the Comando Tlahuica criminal group Homero Figueroa Meza “La Tripa” was arrested by federal agents in connection to the murder of Flores Soberante. Sandra León Varo was also arrested in the same operation.

Flores Soberanes's widow and their four daughters were placed under the federal Protection Mechanism, although the Ministry of the Interior sought to withdraw protection in October 2024. The killing prompted thousands to march in memory of Flores Soberante in Mexico City, and drew condemnation from Amnesty International, Cultural Survival, ARTICLE 19, and other international human rights organisations.

Santiago Barroso Alfaro, aged 47, was a journalist, radio host, and director of the news portal Red 653 in San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora. He hosted the radio programme San Luis Hoy on 91.1 FM Río Digital and was a contributor to the weekly publication Contraseña. The IFJ reported that Barroso had denounced the presence of individuals linked to human trafficking and drug trafficking in Sonora the day before he was killed.

On the night of 15 March 2019, a gunman shot Barroso at the entrance of his home. He was able to call an ambulance but died at a local hospital around 11:00 p.m. Sonora state authorities subsequently characterised the killing as a crimen pasional (crime of passion) and arrested the suspected perpetrator within one week. However, fellow journalist Rafael Cano Franco publicly stated that Barroso’s killing was linked to his journalistic work, and PEN America urged authorities to conduct a thorough investigation including possible links to Barroso’s professional activities. A court sentenced Omar “N” to 22 years in prison for qualified homicide through an abbreviated procedure.

Telésforo Santiago Enríquez was an Indigenous community radio journalist and education teacher based in San Agustín Loxicha, Oaxaca. He was the founder and director of the community radio station El Cafetal (Estéreo Cafetal 98.7 FM — “La Voz Zapoteca”), through which he promoted Indigenous rights and Zapotec culture and language. He was also a teacher affiliated with Section 22 of the teachers’ union. He often criticised local authorities in his radio programmes; the day before he was killed, he had taken calls from listeners on the topic of local politicians and embezzlement.

Santiago Enríquez had received death threats in February 2019, which he and individuals close to him believed originated from the brother of San Agustín Loxicha Mayor Pedro Vázquez. His niece confirmed that he had been threatened during an on-air call to his live programme. On 2 May 2019, Santiago Enríquez was ambushed and shot while driving to host his afternoon newscast in the neighbourhood of Ampliación de las Tres Cruces in San Agustín Loxicha. His body, bearing gunshot wounds, was found inside his vehicle. The Oaxaca state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation for qualified homicide. UNESCO’s Director-General condemned the murder and emphasised the importance of community media. The Washington Post noted that he was killed on the eve of World Press Freedom Day. As of the most recent available reporting, the case remains unresolved.

Francisco Romero Díaz, known as “Ñaca Ñaca,” was a citizen journalist in Solidaridad, Quintana Roo, who founded the Facebook-based media outlet Ocurrió Aquí. He began his career by live-streaming local crime scenes and was mentored by Rubén Pat, alongside whom he co-founded the weekly newspaper Playa News in 2016. Pat was himself killed in 2018. After the death of his mentor, Romero was transferred out of Quintana Roo for several months due to safety concerns. Romero was known for live broadcasts from crime scenes, often being the first journalist to arrive, and worked alongside colleagues who shared scoops to avoid putting any single reporter at further risk.

Romero was threatened for his journalistic work on at least five occasions. In early March 2019, he was arbitrarily detained by municipal police while covering a traffic accident and subsequently threatened by a municipal police commander. In April 2019, he was kidnapped by three individuals while covering another accident, blindfolded, tied up, beaten, and abandoned. He filed a complaint with the state prosecutor’s office and released a video holding Solidaridad Mayor Laura Beristaín responsible for whatever might happen to him. ARTICLE 19 contacted the Mechanism the same month, which granted him a panic button and two bodyguards as protective measures. On 7 May 2019, he received death threats against him and his family via private Facebook message.

On 16 May 2019, Romero’s body was found next to his motorcycle in the parking lot of a bar, three blocks from the state police base in Solidaridad. He had been shot by unknown assailants. By 17 May, a suspect had been detained who confessed to receiving telephone instructions to carry out the killing. The state attorney general stated that investigators were probing a network of hired gunmen who received orders and payment by telephone. The suspect indicated the callers claimed affiliation with the CJNG, though prosecutors believed they were likely a local group. Romero was the fourth journalist murdered in Mexico despite having been granted protective measures by the Mechanism.

José Luis Álvarez Flores, known as “Tío Guato” or “Don José,” was an environmentalist leader and founder of the conservation organisation UMA Saraguato, which he established in 2012 to protect a 345-hectare area in Chablé, Tabasco, where he conserved howler monkeys native to southeastern Mexico. He had been threatened with death multiple times—including as recently as the week before his killing—for reporting complaints against a criminal gang’s illegal extraction of sand from the Usumacinta River. Despite multiple requests for protection from the state, authorities never responded to his requests.

His bullet-ridden body was found on the side of a highway between Tabasco and Chiapas near the Calatraba ejido, along with a series of cardboard signs containing threatening messages against his family and his top collaborators. The Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources publicly expressed outrage over his murder. His case remains unresolved.

Norma Sarabia was a correspondent for Tabasco Hoy and the secretary of the Ramón Herrera elementary school in Villa Chontalpa, Huimanguillo, Tabasco, where she hoped to become a teacher. She was 46 years old and was about to graduate from the University of Chontalpa with a degree in psychology before her death. Sarabia covered local crime and politics, particularly fuel theft near the federal Cárdenas-Coatzacoalcos highway. In the week preceding her death, Tabasco Hoy published a report without a cited byline accusing Mayor José del Carmen Torruco of corruption and nepotism in the Municipal Police Department, headed by Marino Reyes Delgado. CPJ reported that in 2014 Sarabia had reported to state authorities receiving threats from local police officers after she covered the alleged involvement of police in kidnappings. Media reports further indicated that she had received multiple death threats and feared for her life.

On the evening of 11 June 2019, at approximately 9:30 p.m., Sarabia was shot by two armed men as she entered her home on Nicolás Bravo Avenue, in the Club Liberal neighbourhood. Her body was found at the bottom of the stairs. The Tabasco State Attorney General opened an investigation and ordered protection measures for Sarabia’s family members. In December 2020, a man identified as Uriel “N” — a police commander and head of a homicide unit in the Frontera municipality who worked in Huimanguillo — was detained as a suspect. Sarabia had confronted Uriel “N” shortly before her death, accusing him of illegally arresting two teenagers and attempting to extort their families. Notably, the state prosecutor’s office arrested him for alleged extortion and did not publicly mention Sarabia’s killing in connection with his apprehension.

Marcos Miranda Cogco, known as “Marmiko,” was the founder of Noticias A Tiempo, a Facebook-based media outlet in Boca del Río, Veracruz. He specialised in reporting on crime and violence. In a video widely quoted but since deleted that he released after his abduction, Miranda Cogco stated that it was the third time in six to eight years that someone had attacked or attempted to kidnap him, but vowed that he would not be intimidated, declaring that he would continue his criticism of the government.  In the same video, he noted that he suspected the government may have been behind his abduction, citing his critique of the Morena party of Cuitláhuac.

On 12 June 2019, at approximately 8:00 a.m., Miranda Cogco was kidnapped while taking his child to school. Two trucks blocked his vehicle near his home, and armed men abducted him. In a video he posted on his media outlet after being rescued that has since been taken down, he described being taken to a room, stripped naked, photographed, and repeatedly struck in the neck and head. The video was partially preserved by journalist Circo Gomez Leyva in a post on Leyva’s own Facebook page. Police rescued Miranda Cogco later that day by intercepting a suspicious vehicle travelling down a dirt road; a shootout ensued with three apparent captors, who escaped on foot, and Miranda Cogco was discovered tied up in the back of the car. Three firearms were seized at the scene, including an Uzi-type weapon and two revolvers.

Lydia Cacho is a renowned Mexican journalist best-known for her investigative reporting into the sexual exploitation of young girls by Mexican politicians and businessmen, and her international reporting. She is an advocate for girls and women, and is the founder and director of the Centro Integral de Atención a las Mujeres in Cancún, a crisis center and shelter for victims of sex crimes, gender-based violence and trafficking.

At approximately 6:30 p.m. on 21 July 2019, attackers broke into Cacho’s home in Puerto Morelos, Quintana Roo after cutting the security camera cables and disabling the alarm. Attackers killed her two dogs and stole work equipment, including an audio recorder, three cameras, several memory cards, a laptop computer, and ten hard drives with information of high public interest related to cases of pedophilia. Cacho had security protection the night of the attack, but it is unclear if they were assigned through the federal Protection Mechanism.

Following the attack, Cacho immediately left Mexico and went to the United States. In the week after, Cacho says it was determined by Interpol the attackers were sicarios from the Sinaloa cartel. Ricardo Sánchez Pérez del Pozo, head of the office of the Federal Special Prosecutor for Attention to Crimes Committed Against Freedom of Expression, told CPJ that his office had opened an investigation into the burglary. Cacho moved permanently to Spain, where she was naturalized in 2021.

Cacho has been attacked for her reporting for decades. In 1999, Cacho was raped and beaten in the bathroom of a bus station. She suspects the attack was related to her work. She was kidnapped and tortured for 20 hours by state police in 2005 after publishing "The Demons of Eden," her 2005 book that exposed a pedophile ring operating in Puebla and Quintana Roo states. A recording of a conversation between Lebanese businessman Kamel Nacif Borge and then-governor of Puebla Mario Marín Torres that revealed Nacif thanking Torres for arresting Cacho was discovered by the media in 2006. Cacho took these recordings to the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation, where the judges determined in 2007 that the violations of her rights had not been serious.

In 2007, Cacho alleged that her car was tampered with in an attempt to cause an accident. Her bodyguards discovered that the nuts had been loosened on one of the wheels, nearly causing the car to crash. The attack came on 7 May 2007, five days after Cacho appeared at the trial of accused pedophile Jean Succar Kuri, one of the men she wrote about in her 2005 book. In 2009, Cachao was granted protection from the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

In 2018, the UN Human Rights Committee ruled that Cacho's rights had been violated and ordered the Mexican state to re-open the investigation into the attack, and to give her adequate compensation. This judgment has led to several arrests of state agents in Puebla, including a former governor and chief of the judicial police and several police officers. In 2019, just months before the July break-in, the Mexican government publicly apologized to Cacho in an unprecedented ceremony arbited by Alejandro Encinas, Undersecretary of Human Rights.

No update has been provided on Cacho’s case of breaking and entering, and robbery. However, former governor of Puebla Mario Marín, who ordered Cacho’s arrest and torture in 2005, was arrested in 2021. He was released on house arrest during legal proceedings in August 2024, and sent to Altiplano prison in April 2025. As of May 2026, he lost his latest appeal and remains incarcerated in Altiplano prison.

Nidya Hernández was the director of the digital media outlet Domingo 7 in Tehuacán, Puebla. She had been known for speaking out about problems with the government of Ernestina Fernández for three years, and had served briefly as Director of Social Communications for the Fernández administration before resigning over what she perceived as corruption. She had recently criticised former police commanders who were dismissed for corruption involving the municipal government.

On 23 July 2019, at approximately 10:40 p.m., unknown men fired upon her home, which also served as the office for her news outlet. The bullets penetrated a window and the main door, though no one was physically injured. Although Hernández stated she had not received prior direct threats, she believed the attack was connected to her journalistic work, particularly her recent reporting on corruption in the Municipal Public Security Department. She publicly called on the state governor, the governor-elect, and President López Obrador to intervene and investigate the attack.

Rogelio Barragán Pérez, aged 47, was the director of the news outlet Guerrero al Instante. Before founding his own media outlet, he worked for local media including Ecos de Guerrero and Agencia Informativa Guerrero. RSF contacted his colleagues, who revealed that Barragán Pérez had decided to stop signing his articles for security reasons, as had other colleagues at the same outlet.

According to those close to Barragán, he left Chilpancingo, Guerrero around 7:00 p.m. on July 29 to travel to Zacatepec, Morelos to visit his family. Barragán’s family reported losing touch with him after his departure. His body was found on 30 July 2019 inside the trunk of his car at the corner of 21 de Marzo and Circunvalación streets, in the Benito Juárez neighbourhood of Zacatepec, Morelos. According to forensic authorities, the body showed bruises on the face and a lesion in the brain area, indicating he was tortured before death. The Morelos Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation file. The CNDH condemned the killing and demanded a thorough investigation without discarding the victim’s journalistic work as a line of inquiry. The state government activated the protection mechanism for the journalist’s family after his death. Based on the available evidence, no one has been arrested, charged, tried, or convicted for the killing of Barragán Pérez. As of 2 August 2019, the head of FEADLE told CPJ that his office had not opened an investigation into Barragán's murder.

Jorge Celestino Ruíz Vázquez was a journalist in the Actopán region of Veracruz who had reported death threats after being threatened by the Actopán mayor for his reporting on corruption. In 2018, he was the victim of two recorded attacks: on 24 October, his car was beaten with bats; and on 17 November, bullets were fired into his home and car windshield. On 24 October 2018, Ruíz Vázquez was incorporated into the Veracruz State Public Security Secretariat’s security protocol under the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Electoral Crimes and Crimes against Freedom of Expression. He received home protection measures, but no bodyguards. 15 days before his murder, using Ruíz Vázquez’s boss as an  emissary, the mayor attempted to pay off the journalist for damages to his car and home with 10,000 pesos in exchange for dropping charges he had filed against the mayor, an offer he rejected. Days before his murder, he published an article pointing to an alleged embezzlement of 10 to 12 million pesos by José Paulino Domínguez Sánchez, municipal president of Actopán.

On 2 August 2019, Ruíz Vázquez was attacked with a firearm at approximately 9:15 p.m. in a small convenience store he owned in the town of La Bocanita. The Veracruz Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation and announced that it would investigate why the protection measures issued in the victim’s favour were not being complied with. On 8 November 2019, state authorities arrested Facundo “N”—the father of Florencio Barradas, the personal bodyguard of Mayor Domínguez—who allegedly carried out the killing at the mayor’s order. On 5 May 2022, Facundo “N” was sentenced to 32 years in prison. However, both Domínguez and Barradas fled while under investigation and their whereabouts remained unknown as of August 2023.

Edgar Alberto Nava López was a journalist and municipal government official in Zihuatanejo, Guerrero. In October 2018, he was appointed Director of Regulations for the municipal government of Zihuatanejo, while continuing to publish articles including news on local government, crime, and violence. Nava López published his articles on various local media sites as well as his Facebook media outlet La Verdad de Zihuatanejo, which he founded in 2014. According to people who knew him, he was well connected with local politicians; the mayor of Zihuatanejo de Azueta publicly called him “my friend and colleague.” A former colleague of Nava López reported that he had received death threats two months before his death due to his coverage of crime, and that in response he had taken down those stories. Four months before his death, Nava López and other journalists had been threatened as part of an attack against the newspaper Diario de la Costa, to prevent them from publishing further reports on the violence in Zihuatanejo.

On 2 August 2019—the same day as the killing of Jorge Celestino Ruíz Vázquez—Nava López was shot at approximately 10:00 a.m. while on a beach tour with a group of children as part of an activity organised by the City Council. He was killed with a 9mm-calibre firearm, the shell casing of which was seized at the scene. There has been no public report of any  investigation into his murder.

Mitzi Yanet Torres Quintero was a television reporter for CB Televisión, a local news channel in Morelia, Michoacán, covering infrastructure issues, public services, and community affairs. In the early morning hours of 20 August 2019, Torres Quintero was the victim of an attempted sexual assault and called 911 for help. Three municipal police officers arrived at the scene but, according to ARTICLE 19, were persuaded by the aggressor that no assault had occurred. They detained Torres Quintero without explanation. Once inside the patrol car, upon learning she was a journalist, the officers’ physical and verbal violence intensified: they struck her in the face and body, questioned her clothing, and told her that her professional connections would not help her. She was detained for approximately eight hours at the municipal detention centre, where officers mocked her profession, calling her “poor little reporter.” The medical examiner refused to certify her visible injuries or perform a medical examination; several hours later a judge refused to acknowledge her injuries due to the lack of a medical record. Torres Quintero was released and fined by a civic judge for disturbing the peace; having been released before the 24-hour arrest period she was also assigned community service.

The CNDH condemned the police aggressions and the conduct of the medical examiner, and requested precautionary measures to protect Torres Quintero and her family. Three officers were suspended pending investigation, and the Michoacán state prosecutor opened an investigation. However, a judge subsequently declined to bring charges against the three officers, concluding there were not enough elements to link the officers to the allegations of abuse and injury against Torres Quintero. Torres Quintero further reported that following her public denunciation, municipal police officers used fake social media profiles to discredit her account, and the municipal government engaged in a campaign to delegitimize her testimony.

Nevith Condés Jaramillo, aged 42, was the founder and director of El Observatorio del Sur, an online news site based in Tejupilco, Estado de México, which he founded in 2015. He had previously worked as a radio show host and reporter for the local station Radio Roca. His journalism focused on citizen complaints, including coverage of infrastructure failures, hospital medication shortages, flood damage, police extortion, and the failure of elected officials to fulfil campaign promises. Jaramillo also ran a citizen complaint program in Tejupilco called “De Frente al Sur.” He reported on stories in the Tierra Caliente region—an area encompassing communities in Estado de México, Guerrero, and Michoacán—marked by significant violence.

Condés Jaramillo had reported receiving threats on several occasions, including from municipal government officials in Tejupilco. In May 2018, he publicly denounced on video that he had received threats from the then-municipal president, Anthony Domínguez Vargas, stating that since 2017 individuals associated with Domínguez had warned him to cease his reporting or face consequences. In June 2019, he received further threats after breaking the news that a helicopter crash near Sultepec had been caused by gunmen shooting the pilot, which state authorities initially denied and later confirmed. The federal Mechanism attempted to enroll him in a protection scheme in January 2018 and again in June 2019 after receiving requests from ARTICLE 19, but he ultimately declined protection, allegedly due to the onerous bureaucratic procedures and travel involved. Jaramillo did make several reports to the Mechanism after receiving threats from municipal government officials in Tejupilco. Two days before his death, he communicated via WhatsApp that he continued to receive threats from the family of the municipal president.

On 24 August 2019, his body was found in Cerro de Cacalotepec, Tejupilco, bearing multiple stab wounds—with one report indicating as many as 100 stab wounds. His last broadcast for El Observatorio del Sur had been the previous evening. The FGJEM opened an investigation with three lines of inquiry: two related to his journalistic activity and one of a personal nature. ONU-DH condemned the killing and called for a diligent and impartial investigation. UNESCO’s Director-General also condemned the murder. CNDH called for Jaramillo’s family to be assigned protection, and recommended an investigation of his murder in relation to his work as a journalist. In August 2021, journalists in Estado de México protested outside the FGJEM demanding justice. As of August 2025—more than six years after the killing—the FGJEM and FEADLE had not identified any suspects, nor progressed in the investigation.

Paúl Velázquez Benítez was an independent activist and citizen journalist based in Los Mochis, Ahome Municipality, Sinaloa. He operated a YouTube channel and Facebook page titled Ni un corrupto más (“Not one more corrupt official”), through which he published videos criticising local officials and denouncing alleged corruption, particularly in the Ahome municipal government. On 2 April 2019, he attended President López Obrador’s morning press conference and publicly accused the mayor of Ahome, Manuel Guillermo Chapman Moreno, of corruption, including an alleged network of false-invoice companies linked to the tax authority.

On 18 December 2019, a day before the attack, during a municipal event at which Mayor Chapman offered a court-ordered public apology for committing gender-based political violence against the city attorney, event attendees called for Velázquez Benítez’s lynching, and a municipal official reportedly told another journalist that “the next one is Paul.” Velázquez Benítez stated that Mayor Chapman was present and permitted these comments. Additionally, the síndica de la Central, Irma Delgado, reportedly called on her supporters to attack him at the end of the session.

On the evening of 19 December 2019, Velázquez Benítez was shot while in a pharmacy parking lot in central Los Mochis. Security camera footage showed an individual exiting a vehicle, approaching him, and firing at close range toward his head; the bullet struck his neck and mandible area. He survived and re-entered the pharmacy to request help. The bullet exited through one side of his face, and he required multiple surgeries, including maxillofacial reconstruction.

Two Ahome municipal officials, Síndica Irma Delgado Ríos and Participación Ciudadana coordinator Wilfrido Pineda Ruiz, were called to give statements to the state prosecutor under two hypotheses: as witnesses or for inciting hatred and encouraging the attack. Irma Delgado Ríos was publicly reprimanded for her comments by the city council. Velázquez Benítez was in discussion with the Ministry of the Interior regarding enrollment  in the federal Mechanism’s protection programme following the attack, but one year after the attack, Velázquez Benítez noted he was not receiving protection. On 5 February 2020, he appeared at López Obrador’s morning press conference and publicly demanded justice; the president responded that the case would be investigated and impunity would not be tolerated. However, as of December 2020, one year after the attack, Velázquez Benítez reported that the alleged architect of the attack had been identified by the FGR, but no arrests had been made. No publicly reported arrests or charges have been identified to date.

Cristian Pérez Ojeda, also known as Cris Percovich, was the head of the Facebook social media pages Sin Censura Noticias, Inspector Choyero, and La Vox de Los Cabos. He was known for his reporting on corruption and financial mismanagement of the Los Cabos city council, in Baja California Sur. In September 2019, Pérez was fired from his job at the social communication directorate of the council without reason. He filed a labor lawsuit for unfair dismissal.

On 7 January 2020, Pérez received a text message from Héctor Miranda Burgueño, director of social communication for the Los Cabos city council, reading: “Come on! Tone it down a bit in your posts – the boss is already fed up, and I recommend you don't get on her bad side. I’m warning you."

At around 8:15 p.m. on 29 February 2020, Pérez accompanied his wife to close a family business in San José del Cabo. He noticed a light-colored Ford Escape SUV parked close by, and asked his wife to close the business while he walked away from the store to avoid putting her at risk. Two hooded men carrying long guns forced him into the vehicle and drove toward the nearby town of Santa Anita. Once the car was stopped on the outskirts of the town, Pérez was brutally beaten, reporting that his attackers told him "to stop messing around and stop publishing articles," and that they repeatedly told him they were going to kill him for not toning down his articles. Pérez Ojeda ran away from his attackers when they returned to the car to retrieve what he believed to be a knife. He was able to make it to a housing development and get a ride back to San José del Cabo, after which time he went to a hospital. Pérez Ojeda later alleged that he was tricked into signing an initial report of events by local police at the hospital that minimized his attack.

Pérez Ojeda blamed the attack on the mayor of Los Cabos, Armida Castro, a member of the Morena party, and other officials in her administration, including the director of Social Communication, Héctor Manuel Miranda Burgueño, and the director of public safety, Captain Juan José Zamorano. The council denies any orchestration of the attack on Pérez Ojeda.

Pérez Ojeda filed a report on the attack from the hospital; he was reportedly also in conversation with a Protection Mechanism. No information has been shared publicly about any investigation outcomes.

María Elena Ferral Hernández was a veteran journalist with 30 years of professional experience, based in Veracruz. She served as a correspondent for the regional newspapers Diario de Xalapa and El Heraldo de Poza Rica, and was the founder and director of the digital outlet Quinto Poder de Veracruz. Her reporting focused on enforced disappearances, corruption, and abuses of authority in the region, including cases in which local police were implicated.

Ferral’s investigative work placed her in direct conflict with powerful local actors, and she experienced a prolonged pattern of threats and intimidation directly linked to her journalism. In her journalism, she documented the operations of a political network she termed the “Totonacapan Group,” which she identified as being led by the politician Basilio Camerino Picazo.

On 29 March 2016, she reported to authorities a threat by Picazo, who she stated told her he had already “let her live for too long.” Following that threat, the Comisión Estatal para la Atención y Protección a Periodistas (State Commission for the Care and Protection of Journalists, “CEAPP”) assigned her protective measures, including a bodyguard and a GPS device. However, the Veracruz secretary for public security unilaterally withdrew the protection in 2017, without consulting the CEAPP, on the stated ground that Ferral was not making good use of it.

On 30 March 2020, at approximately 2:00 PM, Ferral was leaving a notary office in central Papantla after a meeting with her lawyer when two unidentified men on a motorcycle opened fire on her. According to an anonymous witness account reported by ARTICLE 19, the assailants had been waiting near her car. Ferral suffered eight gunshot wounds, several of which perforated her liver and lung. She was transferred to a hospital and died hours later.

Veracruz judicial authorities detained several individuals and acknowledged that the murder was directly linked to Ferral’s journalistic work. The Veracruz State Attorney General’s Office obtained 30-year prison sentences against three individuals—Carlos “N,” Alfredo “N,” and Othoniel “N”—for the homicide. A fourth individual, Nicasio “N,” was sentenced to 30 years a few weeks later. A fifth individual, José “N,”—identified by the president in a press conference as a crime reporter himself—received a 15-year sentence, and a sixth, Luis Alfonso “N,” was sentenced to 20 years. Critically, despite the Veracruz government’s public allegation that former local deputy Picazo was the intellectual author of the killing, he had not been detained as of this writing. The attack on Ferral was followed by a further assassination attempt: on 24 May 2020, unknown individuals fired upon Ferral’s daughter, María Fernanda De Luna Ferral—who had assumed directorship of Quinto Poder—while she was travelling with state-provided escorts in Gutiérrez Zamora, Veracruz. Fernanda was given protection under the Veracruz Public Security Secretariat (SSP) following the attack, and was enrolled in the federal Mechanism in 2020. Her protection under SSP was revoked on 20 February 2026, without a stated reason. On 28 February 2024, a civil judge ordered the release of one of the alleged perpetrators of Ferral’s murder not yet sentenced. A year later on 28 August 2025, a second alleged perpetrator was released under an injunction arguing the lack of evidence against him.

On 14 April 2020, journalists Hugo García Cambrón and Ernesto Álvarez Avendaño were beaten and arbitrarily detained by officers of the Secretaría de Seguridad Ciudadana (SSC) while covering a fatal traffic accident in the Central de Abasto, Mexico City. Video footage of the officers assaulting the journalists circulated on social media, prompting the SSC to announce the suspension of two officers involved and to issue a public statement condemning attacks on media professionals. The incident illustrated the vulnerability of journalists to physical violence by state security forces, even in the national capital, during the exercise of routine coverage.

Jorge Miguel Armenta Ávalos was the director general and owner of Grupo Editorial Medios Obson, which published the daily newspaper El Tiempo, the weekly magazine Semanario Última Palabra, and associated digital platforms in Cajeme, Sonora. He was also described as a radio announcer and artistic promoter.

Armenta had been enrolled in the federal Protection Mechanism since 2016, following the onset of threats against him. His protection measures were reinforced following a 2019 risk assessment. A crime reporter at El Tiempo told CPJ that Armenta and members of his editorial staff had received numerous threats in recent years from criminal organizations angered by the outlet’s reporting on killings in Ciudad Obregón.

On the afternoon of 16 May 2020, at approximately 3:30 PM, unidentified armed men opened fire on Armenta and two Cajeme municipal police officers serving as his bodyguards under the mechanism as they left a restaurant on Calle Chihuahua in Colonia Centro, Ciudad Obregón. Armenta and one bodyguard, Orlando Antonio Ruvalcaba Flores, died during transport to the Hospital General de Cajeme. A second officer, Cruz Rafael “N,” was injured. The Sonora Attorney General stated that no line of investigation would be ruled out, and investigators recovered spent casings indicating the use of multiple weapons of different calibres.

The killing was condemned by the CNDH, ONU-DH, and a joint statement of the EU delegation in Mexico together with Norway and Switzerland, which noted that Armenta was under the protection of the federal mechanism at the time of the attack and urged an expeditious and transparent investigation. As of September 2025—more than five years after the killing—Medios Obson published a column noting that 1,953 days had passed and describing the case as remaining in total impunity. No arrests, charges, or convictions have been publicly reported.

Marco Antonio Duarte Vargas is the founder and editor of the online news outlet Ciudad Obregón Sin Censura, which publishes on Facebook and focuses on corruption and abuses by local authorities in Cajeme, Sonora. Duarte Vargas had experienced a sustained campaign of intimidation prior to the attack. In August 2019, he received death threats from Ascensión López Durán, a Cajeme municipal official, in connection with his reporting. In October 2019, unknown individuals stole cameras and computers from his home and poisoned one of his dogs. In December 2019, two individuals threatened him with shooting, after which another of his dogs was found dead. He took down a separate news website following these threats. Duarte Vargas had been in contact with the federal Protection Mechanism to seek enrollment, but protection had not materialised as of May 2020.

On 27 May 2020, at approximately 11:30 PM, unknown assailants used a Molotov cocktail to set fire to Duarte Vargas’s car while it was parked in the garage of his residence; he and his family were inside the home at the time. The Sonora state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation. Duarte Vargas noted that the Sonora State Public Security Secretariat assigned patrols to his home as a security measure in consequence to the attack, but that they ceased by June 2. In a further act of apparent retaliation, Duarte Vargas and a colleague, Miguel Valdez Miranda, were detained on 30 June 2020 on fabricated extortion charges. They were imprisoned for eleven months and twelve days before a judge ruled on 12 July 2021 that there was no evidence for the alleged extortion and absolved them. On 28 April 2023, a federal judge ordered two Sonora state prosecutors, Roberto Quintanar Rivas and Carlos Andrés Jaime López, to issue a public apology to Duarte Vargas and Valdez Miranda for impeding their communication with family and counsel during detention.

Pablo Morrugares Parraguirre, aged 48, was the founder and editor of PM Noticias, a digital news outlet covering politics, security, and crime in Iguala, Guerrero. Before founding PM Noticias, Morrugares had worked as a spokesperson for the Iguala municipal government during the mayoral administration of José Luis Abarca, who was arrested on 4 November 2014 for his alleged involvement in the mass abduction and suspected assassination of 43 students from the Escuela Normal Rural de Ayotzinapa on 26 September 2014. In August 2022, the Comisión para la Verdad y Acceso a la Justicia del Caso Ayotzinapa (CoVAJ) identified Morrugares as one of 26 key individuals killed in the preceding eight years who had possessed information about the 2014 mass disappearance.

Morrugares had been enrolled in the federal Protection Mechanism since 2015. On 7 April 2016, he and his wife survived an armed attack by unidentified gunmen in Iguala. Following that attack, the Mechanism relocated him to a safe house at an undisclosed location in 2018, where he remained under federal protection until the end of 2019. He returned to Iguala at his own request in January 2020 and was assigned two state police officers as bodyguards. In the months before the killing, Morrugares was threatened in a Facebook video allegedly posted by a criminal gang active in the Iguala area, and on a narcomanta—a banner used by criminal groups to convey messages—that also named other local reporters.

Just before 1:00 AM on 2 August 2020, Morrugares opened the PM Noticias Facebook page and began a live broadcast from “Búfalos,” the restaurant he owned in central Iguala, discussing violence attributed to the criminal group Los Tlacos in nearby Huitzuco. Recently, Morrugares had published a piece on the detention of two suspects in a homicide case, and another on an ambush on police forces by organized crime. Minutes after the broadcast ended, occupants of a vehicle arrived at the establishment and opened fire. Investigators recovered 55 shell casings of .223 calibre from AR-15 assault rifles. Two heavily armed men entered the restaurant and killed Morrugares instantly. State police officer Roberto Hernández, assigned as Morrugares’s bodyguard through the Mechanism, was also killed.

The ONU-DH condemned the killing and called for investigation in accordance with international due diligence standards. On approximately 7 August 2020, the Guerrero state Fiscalía arrested eight suspects in a safe house near Iguala; a burned vehicle suspected to have been used in the attack was also recovered. One detainee was linked to the homicide through ballistic comparison. Following Morrugares’s killing, local journalists in Iguala were added to a WhatsApp group by individuals believed to be gang members, who issued a barrage of threats. At least four reporters subsequently fled the city, and the newspaper La Tarde ceased its print edition. The community of reporters covering organised crime in Iguala—estimated at approximately 15—dwindled significantly. No conviction has been publicly reported as of the research date.

Juan Nelcio Espinoza Menera was an independent journalist and the creator of the digital outlet El Valedor TV, based in the border city of Piedras Negras, Coahuila. He operated his outlet primarily through a Facebook page, publishing news and live broadcasts covering local events, violence, and public security. ONU-DH noted that the journalist’s family had alleged prior aggressions or threats by police agents linked to his journalistic activity.

On the evening of 20 August 2020, following an attack on state police in Piedras Negras that triggered a major security mobilisation, Espinoza Menera and fellow journalist Néstor Guerra were conducting a live broadcast covering the violent incidents. In the early hours of 21 August, the two journalists were detained by state police at a checkpoint on Bulevar Mar de Cortés. Authorities claimed the journalists had verbally and physically confronted officers and were allegedly intoxicated. The Coahuila state prosecutor, Gerardo Márquez, initially stated that Espinoza Menera’s death was caused by broncoaspiración (obstruction of airways) and characterised it as a natural cause. However, medical personnel at Hospital General Doctor Salvador Chavarría reported that Espinoza Menera’s body bore signs of torture and a knife wound to the throat, and that he had been brought to the facility in two unmarked vehicles by Fiscalía General del Estado agents. Néstor Guerra, detained simultaneously, was subsequently released.

ONU-DH called on authorities to investigate in accordance with the Minnesota Protocol on the Investigation of Potentially Unlawful Death. The CNDH issued an acuerdo de atracción (attraction agreement) to investigate possible human rights violations. Espinoza Menera’s mother filed a complaint with the FGR on 26 August 2020; on 31 August 2020, FGR forensic personnel exhumed the body and conducted an autopsy under the Minnesota Protocol. On 2 November 2021, ARTICLE 19 announced it had obtained evidence confirming that Espinoza Menera was tortured, presumably by state authorities, and formally added him to its list of journalists killed in connection with their work. In April 2022, the FGR determined that Espinoza Menera was the victim of torture and homicidio calificado (aggravated homicide) perpetrated by police officers of Piedras Negras, and that the killing was carried out with the purpose of punishing the exercise of journalism and freedom of expression. Arrest warrants were obtained against the material perpetrators. The FGR also obtained the vinculación a Proceso (formal charging) of the former coordinator of Servicios Periciales of the Coahuila state Fiscalía for cover-up of torture, issuance of false forensic reports, document alteration, and concealment of evidence—having manipulated autopsy records to simulate that Espinoza Menera died of respiratory problems upon arrival at the hospital.

Julio Valdivia Rodríguez, aged 41, was a correspondent for the daily newspaper El Mundo de Córdoba, based in the municipality of Tezonapa, Veracruz. He had worked for El Mundo since 2014, covering a broad range of issues, though his most recent reporting focused heavily on crime and security. Colleagues described him as dedicated, covering stories at any hour; when his income from journalism was insufficient, he supplemented it by working as a bricklayer or selling tamales.

In 2015, Valdivia received protective measures from the State Commission for the Attention and Protection of Journalists (CEAPP) following the killing of his colleague Armando Saldaña Morales, also from Tezonapa. However, the measures were subsequently withdrawn. Although the CEAPP stated Valdivia had not reported any threats, colleagues told Animal Político that he had informed them on various occasions about threats he had received due to his journalistic work. A colleague told the press that Valdivia had recounted being kidnapped and intimidated on multiple occasions because of his crime reporting, but continued because of his passion for journalism.

On 9 September 2020, Valdivia told a colleague he was leaving his residence on the newspaper-provided motorcycle to report on a story. His last published report, dated 7–8 September 2020, covered a shootout involving police and a criminal group in Oaxaca. His body was discovered at approximately 2:30 PM, decapitated, on the train tracks in the locality of Motzorongo, roughly eight kilometres from Tezonapa. His motorcycle, bearing the El Mundo logo, was found nearby. The body showed signs of torture. Forensic analysis indicated that Valdivia had been killed elsewhere and his body subsequently transported to the train tracks, where his motorcycle was also placed. Indeed, the Veracruz state attorney’s office initially stated that the death would be ruled an accident, but reversed course after forensic experts ruled out that possibility, stating that it would investigate the killing as a homicide, with the victim’s journalism as a line of inquiry.

ONU-DH, the UN Secretary-General, UNESCO, and RSF all condemned the killing. According to Mexico News Daily,  Valdivia was the 25th journalist killed in Veracruz since 2010 and the third during the administration of Governor Cuitláhuac García Jiménez. On 31 March 2022—eighteen months after the killing—a multi-agency operation arrested Gustavo Abigaíl Díaz (“El Pino”), identified as a leader of the CJNG in the Veracruz–Oaxaca border region. On approximately 7 April 2022, the Veracruz Fiscalía obtained a vinculación a Proceso against El Pino for homicidio doloso calificado. Federal security secretary Rosa Icela Rodríguez publicly identified El Pino as the son of former PRI state deputy Gustavo Díaz Sánchez (“El Gato”), who was himself arrested in November 2021. No final sentence or conviction has been publicly reported to date.

Víctor Manuel Jiménez Campos, aged 38 and known by the nicknames “El Gordo” and “Vic,” was an independent journalist based in Celaya, Guanajuato, specialising in crime reporting. He worked for the Facebook-based news pages Nota Roja de Celaya Guanajuato, Digital Noticias, and Rotativa Digital de Guanajuato, as well as the portal Informativo Ágora, covering crime and security for approximately four years in a region marked by extreme violence between the CJNG and the Santa Rosa de Lima Cartel.

On the afternoon of 1 November 2020, Jiménez Campos left his home to cover a baseball game in the community of Elguera, on the border between the municipalities of Celaya and Villagrán. He stopped responding to messages during or after his time at the event. His disappearance was reported on 4 November 2020. In the days following, friends and colleagues organised search parties in surrounding agricultural fields and found a shirt and a tennis shoe belonging to Jiménez Campos, both stained with blood.

Three years and seven months after his disappearance, on 10 June 2024, the state attorney general of Guanajuato informed Jiménez Campos’s family that skeletal remains had been discovered and identified as his through DNA analysis. His remains were found inside an abandoned water well in the community of San Salvador de Torrecillas, municipality of Villagrán; the site functioned as a clandestine grave, as additional unidentified human remains were also found there. The prosecutor’s office did not publicly disclose the cause of death. On 5 March 2025, the Guanajuato FGE determined there was no evidence connecting Jiménez Campos’s murder  to his journalistic work. No arrests or convictions have been reported.

Israel Vázquez Rangel, aged 31, was a reporter for the digital news portal El Salmantino, based in Salamanca, Guanajuato. He had worked at the outlet for approximately three years and primarily covered crime and public security.

In the early morning of 9 November 2020, Vázquez received a tip about the discovery of human remains left in plastic bags on a street in the Colonia Villa Salamanca 400. Vázquez drove to the scene in predawn darkness, arriving before any police officers, and approached on foot. As he prepared to broadcast a Facebook Live stream for El Salmantino, armed assailants arrived and shot him at least five times, including when he was already on the ground. National Guard units responded to the shooting, and called in support from the Red Cross to transfer Vázquez to receive medical attention. He was transported to Hospital Regional PEMEX, where he died during or after surgery around midday. The subsequent FGR investigation determined that the remains had been deliberately placed as a lure to draw the journalist to the location. Neither Vázquez nor El Salmantino had reported receiving threats, and the Federal Mechanism confirmed it had not been aware of any threats against either.

ONU-DH condemned the killing, noting Vázquez was the second journalist killed in Mexico within days of the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists. Local journalists protested outside the Ayuntamiento in Salamanca demanding justice. In a widely denounced response, Salamanca mayor María Beatriz Hernández Cruz stated that journalists sometimes “take too many risks” and questioned why Vázquez went to a dangerous neighbourhood without police present.

Six days after the attack, the Guanajuato state Fiscalía detained two suspects: Martín Eduardo López Orozco (“El Tacones”) and José Luis Martínez Aguilera (“El Pizzero”). The FGR’s FEADLE subsequently attracted the investigation to the federal level. On 14 December 2021, López Orozco was sentenced to 20 years in prison after entering a guilty plea; the judge stated the homicide was committed with the objective of limiting Vázquez’s freedom of expression. On 7 September 2023, Martínez Aguilera was found guilty of Vázquez’s murder. FEADLE presented evidence demonstrating that the accused, along with López Orozco, lured the journalist to a predetermined location to assault him as retaliation for a news article in which he published the face of a criminal leader in the area. On 14 September 2023, Martínez Aguilera was sentenced to 27 years and 6 months in prison and ordered to pay reparación integral del daño to Vázquez’s daughters. However, the judge ruled that Vázquez’s status as a journalist was not a determinative factor in the sentencing, indicating there was not enough evidence pointing to Vázquez’s work as a motive. FEADLE, which had requested the maximum 35-year sentence, announced an appeal. CPJ welcomed the conviction but expressed concern that the journalistic motive was not recognised.

Jaime Daniel Castaño Zacarías was a photojournalist and the director of the digital news portal Prensa Libre MX, based in Jerez, Zacatecas. He had approximately 20 years of professional experience, having previously worked for the regional newspaper El Sol de Zacatecas, and also served in the public communications office of the Jerez municipal government.

On the morning of 9 December 2020, Castaño Zacarías attended a municipal government event and, while returning, encountered the bodies of two men on Federal Highway 23. The victims displayed bound hands, gunshot wounds, visible signs of torture, and a narcomensaje. Police had not yet arrived at the scene. Two journalistic sources told ARTICLE 19 that armed individuals at the scene confronted the journalist about the photographs he had taken and demanded he delete them. Castaño Zacarías refused to surrender or delete his photographs, mounted his motorcycle, and departed. A few kilometres further on, occupants of another vehicle caught up with him and opened fire, killing him. The gunmen then removed the memory card from his camera. According to the mayor's office, Castaño Zacarías was attended to by Civil Protection personnel, who confirmed his death.

ARTICLE 19 stated it had no evidence of prior threats or intimidation against him before his killing. ONU-DH condemned the killing, with its representative in Mexico stating that the attack was an assault on Mexican society as a whole. UNESCO Director-General Audrey Azoulay called on Mexico to investigate and bring the perpetrators to trial. ARTICLE 19 called on FEADLE to attract the case and apply the Protocolo Homologado de Investigación de Delitos contra la Libertad de Expresión. Local journalists and civil society groups organised a protest on 11 December 2020 demanding justice. Despite the case being considered the first killing of a journalist in Zacatecas since 2014, no subsequent public follow-up occurred, and it remained unclear whether federal authorities were involved in the investigation. No arrests or convictions have been reported.

Jorge Molontzín Centlal was a journalist who worked as a reporter for the Semanario Confidencial, a weekly news magazine and website based in the town of Caborca, in the northern Mexican state of Sonora. Originally from the state of Chiapas, Molontzín had spent over twelve years covering the municipalities of the Sonoran Desert. His reporting focused on public works, local politics, and social affairs. He also distributed copies of the magazine throughout the region and supplemented his journalistic income by selling products—such as car windshields and sacks of potatoes—during his travels, using those trips to gather information from local authorities for his reporting.

Confidencial’s editor, José Alfredo Gastón Gastélum, told CPJ that the magazine had “mostly stopped publishing stories about crime” after receiving threats over its coverage several years prior, though no recent threats had been reported and Gastón Gastélum was unaware of threats specifically targeting Molontzín. An official of the federal Protection Mechanism confirmed to CPJ that the Mechanism had not been in contact with Molontzín and was unaware of any threats against him.

On the morning of 10 March 2021, Molontzín was driving a red pickup truck from the town of Benjamín Hill toward Santa Ana, accompanied by his friend Eudocio Cruz Méndez, a horticulturist from Puebla who frequently accompanied him on his travels. Confidencial’s editor spoke with him that morning; his nephew, attorney Lázaro Molontzín, stated the journalist last communicated with his family at approximately 2:00 PM. After their last known contact, calls to the mobile phones of both Molontzín and Cruz Méndez went directly to voicemail. Neither man has been seen or heard from since. Colleagues at Confidencial presumed the two men had been forcibly taken.

Confidencial published a statement on 17 March 2021 publicly denouncing the disappearance and requesting government action. A spokesperson for the Sonora state prosecutor’s office confirmed to CPJ that an investigation had been opened. As of September 2024, LatAm Journalism Review reported that Molontzín Centlal remained among five journalists still missing from the López Obrador administration period. No arrests, charges, or convictions in connection with the disappearance have been publicly reported.

Pablo Felipe Romero Chávez was a journalist based in Guaymas, Sonora, who worked as a crime reporter (“nota roja”) for the radio station FM 105.3 and the newspaper El Vigía, both of which belonged to the Grupo Padilla Hermanos media conglomerate. Romero Chávez was 33 years old at the time of his disappearance, had earned a degree in criminology, and had begun working as a reporter at a local radio station approximately six years prior. After an initial period in journalism, he took a three-year hiatus to manage a funeral home before returning to crime reporting in February 2021—only one month before his disappearance.

No specific prior threats, surveillance measures, or enrollment in a protection programme pertaining to Romero Chávez individually have been documented in available reporting. His disappearance occurred in the context of a broader pattern of violence against journalists in Sonora: he was the second journalist to disappear in the state in March 2021, following the disappearance of Jorge Molontzín Centlal fifteen days earlier.

Family members and colleagues lost all communication with Romero Chávez on the morning of 25 March 2021. His grandmother went to his home in the Colonia Las Palmas neighbourhood of Guaymas at approximately 8:00 a.m. and found the doors of the house wide open and his vehicle parked in front, unlocked; his mobile phone was switched off and he could not be reached. The Fiscalía General de Justicia del Estado de Sonora confirmed on 26 March 2021 that it had received the disappearance report and opened an investigation. The Colectivo Guerreras Buscadoras de Sonora, a civilian search collective, published an informational flyer to assist in locating him. On 30 March 2021, a virtual meeting was held between Sonora state government officials and representatives of the Federal Protection Mechanism, out of concern for the disappearance of Romero Chávez and Jorge Molontzín Centlal, who disappeared fifteen days prior. In May 2021, Romero Chávez’s mother publicly appealed for information, describing the period since his disappearance as a “nightmare.”

As of September 2024, Romero Chávez remained among five journalists still missing from the López Obrador administration period. No arrests, charges, or convictions in connection with his disappearance have been publicly reported.

Gabriela Lizeth Talamante Cázarez, known publicly as “Katana Cázarez,” was a 37-year-old radio broadcaster and social media content creator based in Magdalena de Kino, Sonora. She worked at the radio station Casa de Toño and operated a social media news page called La Vox, through which she published local news content.

On 10 April 2021, while en route to her workplace, a man intercepted Talamante Cázarez as she was boarding her vehicle, forced her at gunpoint to drive to a location on the outskirts of the city, threatened her specifically over her creation of the news page La Vox, demanded she shut down her social media accounts, and then subjected her to a severe physical assault. A video subsequently published on social media and since deleted, showed her with multiple contusions on her face, arms, legs, and mouth. Following the attack, her personal social media accounts and the La Vox page were taken down—a direct and successful act of censorship through violence.

The Sonora state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation into the physical assault, classifying the offences as injuries, threats, and robbery; however, the attacker responsible for the 10 April 2021 assault has not been publicly identified or apprehended. The office undertook the investigation as gender violence, assault, intimidation, extortion, and an attack on freedom of expression, with the perpetrator potentially facing a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison.

Benjamín Morales Hernández was the founder and director of Noticias Xonoidag, a Facebook-based news page with approximately 14,000 followers that he had created in 2014 and through which he published video reporting and commentary on current events in the Sonoyta area of Sonora, near the United States border. The Associated Press described his coverage as including community events, police activity, and crime.

On the evening of 2 May 2021, Morales’ family lost contact with him at approximately 19:00 in Sonoyta after he had covered a campaign event for Julio Casanova, a candidate for mayor. Municipal police subsequently located his abandoned white pickup truck with the keys in the ignition near Ejido Morelia. The National Guard found his body at kilometre 165+200 on the Caborca–Sonoyta highway; he had sustained multiple gunshot wounds. Police reported that a piece of cardboard bearing a message had been left with his body. The day before his abduction, Morales had publicly denounced receiving anonymous threats through social media in a since-deleted video posted to his Facebook page. However, a Protection Mechanism official told CPJ that they had not been made aware of threats against him and had not communicated with him prior to his death. No protection measures were in place.

The Sonora State Attorney General’s Office stated it was investigating multiple lines of inquiry, including personal, family, and work-related hypotheses. CPJ reported that it sent several requests for comment to the Sonora prosecutors and received no replies. ONU-DH and UNESCO condemned the killing. No arrests or convictions in connection with Morales’s murder have been publicly reported.

Gustavo Sánchez Cabrera was the director of the news website Noticias Minuto a Minuto and the television channel Panorama Pacífico TV, both based in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec region of Oaxaca. He reported primarily on local politics and crime.

The case of Sánchez Cabrera constitutes one of the most extensively documented failures of Mexico’s federal Protection Mechanism. He was first incorporated into the Mechanism in 2014 after receiving death threats but was subsequently removed for unspecified reasons; the Mechanism removed the camera it had installed at Sánchez Cabrera’s home while he was enrolled after it determined he was no longer at risk. On 13 July 2020, he survived an assassination attempt; the Oaxaca Attorney General’s Office issued an arrest warrant against a suspect named Esteban de la Cruz Lagunas, but the warrant was voided on 30 November 2023 and a new one was not requested until 13 March 2021. Following this attack, Sánchez requested  re-enrollment into the Mechanism, but his case was not evaluated until January 2021. According to RSF, a protection plan for Sánchez Cabrera was validated in May 2021; and protection measures—including cameras outside his home, a personal escort, and a bulletproof vest—were approved on 1 June 2021. None of these measures were implemented before his killing, sixteen days later. RSF reported that it had pressed the Mechanism to provide the promised protection up to the day before Sánchez Cabrera was murdered. Sánchez Cabrera himself also emailed the Mechanism the day before his murder requesting his protective measures be enforced; he was told that “the notifications corresponding to the protection plan set out by the government board have been made. We’re on time for said measures to be implemented.”

At approximately 8:00 on 17 June 2021, while Sánchez Cabrera was riding a motorcycle near the town of Morro Mazatán with his 15-year-old son, two unidentified individuals in a car deliberately crashed into the motorcycle. After Sánchez and his son fell, the assailants exited the vehicle and shot Sánchez Cabrera, killing him with a bullet to the head. At least fifteen 9mm cartridge casings were recovered at the scene. Sánchez’s son sustained mild injuries from the fall but was not shot.

The Oaxaca state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation. ONU-DH condemned the killing and called on authorities to investigate promptly. On 17 June 2024—three years after the murder—the Government of Oaxaca issued a public apology to Sánchez’s family, formally acknowledging that his death could have been prevented had the State provided adequate protection. CNDH concluded that the Mechanism had been negligent. On 20 August 2024, the General Inspector of the Oaxaca State General Attorney’s Office ruled that two prosecutors had been negligent in their professional duties to Sánchez Cabrera following his July 2020 assassination attempt. It was determined that the lack of follow-up in issuing a second arrest warrant left Sánchez Cabrera unprotected, and that there was no meaningful attempt to implement protective measures.

In total, Sánchez Cabrera had received fourteen threats and acts of intimidation, requested government protection on seventeen occasions, and survived four prior attacks before his killing. On 30 April 2025, a suspect identified as Esteban “C” was finally linked to proceedings for the July 2020 attempted homicide against Sánchez Cabrera.

Felipe Enrique García García, also known as “Kike,” was a journalist and communicator from the Estado de México who had worked for El Sol de Toluca and held institutional communications roles with the state government and security secretariat. He was also reported to have handled media relations for an incoming mayor. At the time of his killing, García García was supplementing his income by working as a driver for the ride-hailing platform DiDi.

On the evening of 16 June 2021, García García left in his vehicle and was reported missing by family members when he failed to return. His body was found in  his vehicle with gunshot wounds in Metepec. According to the state prosecutor’s investigative account, three people requested a ride via the platform; during the trip, one of the passengers allegedly ordered the others to shoot the driver.

The Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation the day after García García’s murder. ONU-DH stated there was no information about prior threats against García García but called on authorities to advance investigations without discarding the hypothesis that the attack was linked to his journalistic activity. In October 2021, two suspects—Joseph Argenis “N” and Kimberly Isabel “N”—were arrested and linked to proceedings. In May 2023, they were initially sentenced to 47 years of imprisonment. On appeal, Joseph’s sentence was reduced to 43 years and nine months, while Kimberly’s trial was annulled on grounds that the Venezuelan embassy was not notified of her arrest, violating her consular rights. In 2024, the retrial was extended to both defendants on grounds that their trial was not held within a reasonable time. As of February 2025, the journalist’s wife, Carolina Rodríguez, publicly denounced that two key witnesses had failed to appear at the retrial, a forensic doctor and an eyewitness, raising concerns that the accused might be released.

Saúl Tijerina Rentería was a freelance media worker based in Ciudad Acuña, Coahuila, who provided drone footage and photography to the Facebook-based news outlets La Policiaca and Noticias en la Web. His coverage generally encompassed sports, crime, and security matters. He combined his journalistic work with employment at a local maquiladora assembly plant.

Editors of both outlets told CPJ they were not aware of direct threats to Tijerina’s life, though they indicated he had had “problems” with two coworkers at the factory whom they believed may have had ties to a drug trafficking gang. The LA Times reported that Saúl Tijerina Rentería repeatedly sought help from the Protection Mechanism days before he was murdered, having received death threats due to his reporting; his request went unanswered. ARTICLE 19 highlighted that the precarious economic conditions in which many Mexican journalists work—forcing them to hold second or third jobs—not only increases their exposure to risk but also creates opportunities for authorities to “stigmatize or revictimize” them by arguing they were not truly journalists.

Tijerina disappeared after leaving his factory shift in the early morning hours of 22 June 2021. His body was found later that morning near his vehicle in Ciudad Acuña with multiple stab wounds to the neck. Other reporting claims Tijernia was found tied up in the trunk of his car. A narcomensaje was found with his body, reading: “This is what will happen to all the snitches in the state or those who collaborate with the state. CDN”—a reference to the Cartel del Noreste, a splinter group of the Zetas.

The Coahuila state prosecutor quickly announced the detention of two suspects—Lorenzo “N” and Jordi Alejandro “N”—alleged members of a criminal gang, on 24 June 2021. In a 25 June 2021 press conference, the prosecutor stated his office had not ruled out Tijerina’s media work as a possible motive but was also investigating whether Tijerina had a relationship with the gang. There have been no public updates on the investigation status beyond the initial arrests in 2021.

Abraham Mendoza Mendoza was a radio journalist in Morelia, Michoacán, who had worked for Voces Radio since 2013 as news director, producer, and programme host. At the time of his killing, he contributed to the radio programme “Observatorio” on Uve Radio 98.1 FM at the Vasco de Quiroga University and served as a presenter of Panorama Informativo Michoacán of Grupo ACIR. He had previously worked with Radio ACIR, EXA, Central TV, and CB Televisión.
