RSF reported that on social media Mendoza was often outspoken in his criticism of political corruption at the local and federal levels.

On 19 July 2021, at approximately 15:30, Mendoza was shot at close range as he was leaving a gym on Avenida Madero Poniente in the Nueva Valladolid neighbourhood of Morelia. He was getting into his vehicle when a gunman approached and opened fire; a second individual was reported to have been conducting surveillance from a nearby car. An ice-pop vendor at the scene was also wounded by gunfire.

RSF reported that Mendoza had not reported receiving threats recently. ONU-DH’s Puntal “In Memoriam” entry indicated that he did not have protection measures in place. The Michoacán State Attorney General’s Office detained three men on the day of the killing following a search operation. ONU-DH confirmed the detentions on 27 July 2021. In October 2023, a court sentenced two of the accused—José Wilbert G. and Kevin P.—to 35 years and 6 months in prison and ordered payment of reparations. However, although the material perpetrators were convicted, there has been no reported investigation into who may have ordered the killing or whether it was connected to Mendoza’s outspoken criticism of political corruption.

Ricardo Domínguez López was the founder and director of InfoGuaymas, a digital news outlet with more than 300,000 Facebook followers that covered municipal, state, national, and crime news in Guaymas, Sonora. He also served as president of the Asociación Metropolitana de Periodistas Independientes de Guaymas-Empalme and secretary general of the Sindicato Nacional de Redactores de la Prensa (SNRP), Delegación 11.

Domínguez López had been the victim of multiple digital attacks, threats, smear campaigns, and forced internal displacement prior to his killing. He was the president of the Metropolitan Association of Independent Journalists of Guaymas-Empalme. In November 2020, he publicly denounced in a video that the Guaymas municipal police, under the direction of Comisario de Seguridad Pública Andrés Humberto Cano Ahuir, had created fake social media accounts to defame and discredit him and other journalists; he held Cano Ahuir personally responsible for any harm that might come to him. In March 2021, he stated at a press conference that he had received death threats from criminal groups over his reporting and that local police had used a Facebook page to falsely accuse him of having ties to organized crime. The video has since been deleted. He relocated from Guaymas to his native Cajeme due to the threats and filed a formal complaint with the FGR, registered under case number FGR-0000804/2021.

Despite these documented threats, the National Union of Press Workers reported that no protection measures were offered to safeguard him. CPJ reported that repeated attempts to contact the Federal Mechanism went unanswered. State police patrols were reportedly implemented by the Secretaría de Seguridad Pública del Estado, but ARTICLE 19 stated these measures were insufficient.

On 22 July 2021, he was shot and killed in the parking lot of the Ley Marsella shopping centre in the northern part of Guaymas, at approximately 17:00, just metres from the Guaymas municipal police headquarters. ARTICLE 19 reported that a source close to the journalist suspected he had been lured to the location under the pretext of collecting an advertising payment.

On 26 July 2021, the Sonora state prosecutor said her office was investigating whether Domínguez López’s murder was related to his work as a journalist. Several days later, her office confirmed that Cano Ahuir—the police official whom Domínguez López had publicly accused of orchestrating threats—would be investigated as part of the case. On 23 July 2021, about 30 journalists from Cajeme protested Domínguez López’s murder at the State Prosecutor's Office, while other journalists from different parts of the state refused to publish stories for 24 hours  as a form of protest. Cano Ahuir resigned from his position in December 2021, following a separate armed attack outside the Guaymas municipal palace that reportedly targeted him and killed the activist Marisol Cuadras. As of the date of this filing, no arrests or convictions in connection with the killing of Domínguez López have been publicly reported.

Jacinto Romero Flores was a veteran reporter and radio announcer for Ori Stéreo FM in Veracruz, whose coverage focused on politics and crime in the Zongolica/Altas Montañas region. Since 2015, he had also hosted a Facebook programme titled “Un Café con El Enano con Jacinto Romero Flores.”

At about 10:45 AM on 19 August 2021, unidentified attackers in a vehicle shot Romero Flores multiple times while he was driving in a vehicle marked “Prensa,” or “Press,” on Reforma Boulevard in Potrerillo. He died at the scene; his body was found inside his vehicle near the Reforma bridge. Romero Flores had received threatening messages prior to his killing, including messages reported as early as February 2021 warning him to stop writing. La Jornada reported that on the day of the murder, Romero Flores had left his home to collect aid for people in need who had called his radio program to ask for help, raising the possibility that a trap may have been set in advance for him to walk into the attack, since Romero Flores frequently supported his audience this way. CPJ reported that he had been granted protection from state authorities after being threatened that did not include a bodyguard or vehicle escort protections; an official document from March 2021 instructed the authorities to provide protection due to documented threats. ARTICLE 19 confirmed that he had received death threats linked to his journalistic work.

CNDH and UNESCO condemned the murder of Romero Flores. On 12 November 2021, the Veracruz State Attorney General’s Office reported the detention of three suspects, including a municipal councillor-elect and an elected councilman for Ixtaczoquitlán. A judge subsequently ordered pretrial detention and linked them to criminal proceedings. However, in October 2022, all three were released after a court granted amparo relief against the order linking them to proceedings. CPJ’s 2022 global impunity report noted that the suspects were freed due to lack of evidence. The case thus reverted to impunity.

Jesús Manuel González Reyes, aged 55, was the founder, director, and administrator of Portal Morelos Noticias (also known as “Agencia PM Noticias”), a Facebook-based news outlet with approximately 260,000 followers that covered political news, cultural events, crime, and other local affairs in the state of Morelos.

In the June 2021 municipal elections, González Reyes had been a mayoral candidate in Emiliano Zapata municipality for the Partido para el Bienestar; after losing the election, he continued his journalistic work. In the weeks before his death, Portal Morelos Noticias had covered several homicides in and around Cuernavaca. Unnamed colleagues told the media he had been conducting “special investigations” at the time of his killing.

On 28 September 2021, at approximately 4:30 PM, González Reyes was shot and killed on Calle Leandro Valle in the Colonia Miraval neighbourhood of Cuernavaca. According to eyewitness accounts, two men approached him on a motorcycle after he had finished eating at a food stall and shot him with pistols. He died at the scene; casings from 9mm rounds were recovered. The Morelos Prosecutor’s Office reported that González García was carrying his press credentials at the time of the murder, and stated the victim sustained gunshot wounds to the head at close range. RSF described the attack as an “apparent contract killing.”

A federal Mechanism official told CPJ that the agency was not aware of threats to González Reyes and that he had not been enrolled in a protection programme. A joint communiqué from Mexican press associations noted that the state-level protection mechanism in Morelos had not been active since 18 July 2021—more than two months before the killing. ONU-DH condemned the killing, noting it was the sixth journalist homicide and eighth aggression against a journalist that the office had documented in 2021 with a probable link to journalistic activity. UNESCO and the CNDH also condemned the killing. No arrests or convictions in connection with the murder have been reported in available sources.

Fredy Fernando López Arévalo was a veteran journalist with a career spanning nearly four decades, originally from the municipality of Yajalon, Chiapas. He had served as a correspondent in Central America for the newspapers El Universal and El Financiero, worked as regional coordinator for Mexico’s state news agency Notimex, and covered landmark events. At the time of his death, he directed the magazine Revista Jovel and broadcast on XERA-Radio Uno in San Cristóbal de las Casas. His recent publications included reporting on a criminal group known as “MOTONETOS,” and his last post, on 28 October 2021, covered the dismissal of 200 municipal employees by the mayor.

On the evening of 28 October 2021, at approximately 19:45–20:00, López Arévalo was shot and killed outside his home in Colonia Las Rosas as he was unloading items from his vehicle. He was returning with his wife and children from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, where they had celebrated his mother’s birthday. A lone gunman approached, shot him in the head, and fled on a motorcycle. His wife and daughters were present during the attack.

A federal Mechanism official told CPJ the agency was unaware of threats against López Arévalo and that he had not been enrolled in a protection programme. However, a journalist colleague in Chiapas who knew him personally told CPJ that López Arévalo had written about organized crime and drug trafficking in the region and believed the killing was connected to his work. Neighbours reported that, in the days before the attack, a young man had been seen surveilling the area around his home.

The Chiapas state attorney general’s office opened an investigation, and the FGR subsequently assumed jurisdiction over the case. ONU-DH, CPJ, UNESCO, ARTICLE 19, and PEN International all condemned the killing. On 6 January 2022, authorities announced that the bodies of two men identified as the suspected material perpetrators—Jonathan “N” and Eder Ezequiel “N”—had been found in the trunk of a vehicle near the Guatemalan border, wearing clothing bearing the insignia of the CJNG. No intellectual authors of the killing have been publicly identified or charged.

Alfredo Cardoso Echeverría was a photojournalist based in Acapulco de Juárez, Guerrero, and the founder and editor of the online news outlet Las Dos Costas. He had previously worked as a photographer for several media outlets in Acapulco. On 28 October 2021, masked armed men abducted Cardoso from his home in Acapulco. He was found the following day near his residence with at least five gunshot wounds and was transported to the IMSS Regional Hospital for treatment. After undergoing surgery, Cardoso died in hospital on 31 October 2021.

The Guerrero State Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation on 29 October 2021. Governor Evelyn Salgado condemned the killing and stated she had instructed her government to provide protection to Cardoso’s family. On 23 November 2021, a suspect identified as Roberto “N” was arrested. FEADLE took over the case on 17 March 2022. On 9 August 2022, a federal judge sentenced Roberto “N” to 13 years and four months in prison as the material perpetrator of the murder, though it was noted that he was one of several armed men who abducted Cardoso. The FGR determined that “sufficient and effective evidence was found to determine that the murder of the journalist materialized as a reprisal for his journalistic work.” Notably, in January 2025, a judge ordered an ex-municipal police officer in Acapulco de Juárez identified as Jorge “G” to be held in pretrial detention due to his role as the “instigator” of Cardoso’s killing; it was found that Cardoso published several articles criticizing the actions of Jorge “G.”.

José Luis Gamboa Arenas was the founder and general director of the digital news outlets Inforegio and La Noticia, based in the Port of Veracruz. He followed in the footsteps of his journalist father, transitioning into digital media, where he became known for live broadcasts on social media platforms in which he consistently criticized the wave of violence afflicting the state and the extortion of local businesses. Previously, he had been deeply involved in local politics in the port, having been the Municipal Leader of the Revolutionary Youth Front of the Institutional Revolutionary Party. In the months before his murder, Gamboa had intensified his criticism of local authorities, publishing reports accusing municipal officials of colluding with criminal organizations to allow the extortion of protection money in neighbourhoods throughout the port city, naming both the officials and the criminal groups responsible. ARTICLE 19 reported that among his most recent publications were investigative works titled ‘La Guerra por la Narco Política’ and ‘Prospectiva parte 1,’ which documented regional violence and criticized the government’s failure to combat it.

On 10 January 2022, Gamboa was found with multiple stab wounds in the Floresta neighbourhood of the Port of Veracruz. Conflicting press reports indicate that he was either dead upon discovery or died in hospital three days later. Critically, it took four days for his body to be identified. Because his identity and profession were initially unknown, the State Prosecutor’s Office of Veracruz opened an investigation into aggravated homicide with a presumed robbery motive, a classification that may have delayed or prevented the resources needed for an investigation into whether Gamboa’s murder was related to his profession..

On 16 January 2022, the State Commission for the Attention and Protection of Journalists called on the Veracruz state prosecutor’s office to apply the Protocol for the Investigation of Crimes Against Freedom of Expression to Gamboa’s murder. Authorities stated that they had no record of prior threats against Gamboa related to his journalistic work, and CPJ noted that initial press reports suggested the homicide may have occurred during an attempted robbery. Gamboa was not enrolled in any protection programme, and no protection measures were in place at the time of the attack.

In April 2022, Eduardo “N,” a nephew of José Luis Gamboa, was arrested for his murder. Two months after this arrest, López Obrador publicly asserted that the murder was “a family matter” and unrelated to Gamboa’s journalistic work in Veracruz—a characterization that press freedom organizations challenged as premature and dismissive. A second suspect, Sebastián Alejandro “N,” was arrested in connection with the murder in May 2024. The case remains under investigation, and no conviction has been publicly reported as of the date of this report.

Alfonso Margarito Martínez Esquivel was a freelance photojournalist based in Tijuana, Baja California, who specialized in crime scene photography—a beat that placed him in direct and sustained contact with the activities of organized criminal groups operating along the U.S.–Mexico border. According to CPJ, the head of a local Tijuana Cartel cell considered Martínez responsible for publishing photographs on social media that detailed the structure of the criminal gang led by Christian Adán Velázquez José, known as “El Cabo 16.”

On 17 January 2022, Martínez was shot and killed outside his home. He had briefly returned from a reporting assignment and was preparing to depart again when he was ambushed.  According to friends and colleagues, Martínez had reported threats on several occasions in the years preceding his death. An official with the federal Protection Mechanism confirmed to CPJ that the agency had contacted Martínez several times, but that he stopped responding. Alianza de Medios reported that the heavy bureaucracy involved in the enrollment process discouraged Martínez from finalizing materials for incorporation in the protection program. Martínez had sought to enroll in December 2021 after being publicly accused by a social media user of managing Facebook pages that exposed the identities and activities of drug traffickers, placing him at grave risk.

The prosecution’s investigation subsequently determined that on 15 January 2022, “El Cabo 16” had contacted José Ochoa Díaz, alias “El Huesos,” who in turn engaged Adrián Nicolás Ramos, alias “El Uber,” to carry out the killing and video-record the execution. The contracted price for the murder was approximately 40,000 Mexican pesos.

Adrián Nicolás Ramos and José Heriberto Ochoa Díaz were sentenced in December 2022 for the murder, each receiving 25 years. Christian Adán Velázquez José, identified as the individual who ordered the killing, declined a plea agreement and in 2023 announced he would proceed to trial. Press reports indicate that he may also have been involved in the killing of Lourdes Maldonado López, discussed below. The LA Times subsequently reported that the murders of Martínez and Maldonado were more likely driven by political considerations than by purely criminal motives.

Lourdes Maldonado López was a freelance reporter and correspondent for several outlets and the host of the programme Brebaje on Radio Sintoniza Sin Fronteras in Tijuana, Baja California. She had previously worked for Primer Sistema de Noticias, a news outlet owned by Jaime Bonilla Valdez, a wealthy businessman who served as Governor of Baja California from 2019 to late 2021. In her most recent broadcasts, Maldonado covered a range of topics including criticism of municipal government expenditures and the murder of her colleague Margarito Martínez. She had been pursuing an investigation into possible corruption by the previous state government and had, just days before her murder, won a nine-year labour lawsuit against Bonilla’s media company, which would have paid up to 500,000 pesos ($25,000 USD)  in unpaid wages.

In a moment that would become one of the most widely cited episodes in the crisis of press freedom in Mexico, Maldonado addressed AMLO directly at his morning press conference on 26 March 2019, asking him for protection and stating publicly that she feared for her life due to her labour dispute with Jaime Bonilla. She was subsequently enrolled in the Baja California State Journalists Protection Program and received certain precautionary measures, including a panic button, police patrols at her residence at night, and a state patrol escort upon her arrival home—measures specifically tailored to the moment she identified as her most vulnerable: the transition from her car to her home.

On 23 January 2022—barely six days after the murder of Margarito Martínez—Maldonado was shot and killed inside her car as she arrived at her home. The attackers waited for her protection detail to leave before executing the attack, demonstrating both advanced surveillance and awareness of her security arrangements. The killing drew immediate condemnation from the IACHR. In the wake of her murder, then-Governor of Baja California Jaime Bonilla denied ever having threatened Lourdes Maldonado in a radio interview with El Weso de W Radio, saying: “There was only a labor lawsuit, which was for no more than 400 or 500 thousand pesos, which wasn’t enough to kill anyone.”

Regarding federal protection, conflicting accounts persist: the advisor to the State System for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders and Journalists stated that Maldonado was also enrolled in the federal mechanism, while at his 25 January 2022 morning press conference two days after her murder, AMLO stated that Maldonado was not registered in the federal mechanism, a claim echoed by SEGOB.

In February 2022, Erick Eduardo Contreras Ramos, Kevin Alberto Villarino Hernández, and Guillermo Julián Garzón  were arrested for Maldonado’s murder. In October 2022, Contreras Ramos and Villarino Hernández were sentenced to 20 years in prison, while Julián Garzón was sentenced to 24 years as the shooter. According to the Secretariat of Public and Citizen Security, the perpetrators were hired by the Arellano Félix Cartel to kill Maldonado after she reported on the group’s activities. The involvement of the same cartel cell implicated in the Martínez killing raises serious questions about whether these murders were coordinated and whether the protection mechanisms—both state and federal—failed by design or through negligence. In March 2026, a judge charged Jaime Bonilla with embezzlement and abuse of power, after detecting possible irregularities in the handling of public resources during his time as Governor of Baja California. The charges did not relate to the murder of Maldonado, and Bonilla has reportedly not been summoned in the course of the murder investigation. Despite the arrests of Maldonado’s alleged killers, no progress on the investigation has been reported.

Roberto Toledo was a camera operator, photographer, and video editor for Monitor Michoacán, a digital news outlet based in Zitácuaro, Michoacán, that was the only news source in the city that systematically investigated municipal government corruption. The outlet operated from a law office that also financed it. Toledo had published a November 2020 article titled “Cheap Works or Crony Deals?” exposing alleged corruption in public works funded by the municipal government, and his most recent assignment concerned the alleged illicit enrichment of authorities at the Zitácuaro Senior Citizens’ Home. Four days before Toledo’s murder, Monitor Michoacán published a commentary criticizing state authorities for allegedly altering records of individuals arrested on drug possession charges.

On 31 January 2022, Toledo was shot in the courtyard of the law office that housed Monitor Michoacán. He had been returning from a corner store when he was approached by two men who asked him “where the lawyer was,” in reference to Joel Vera Terrazas, whose law office financed the paper. Toledo walked into the courtyard; the men followed and shot him in the torso and forearms, fleeing by motorcycle. Minutes later, one of the killers returned to the crime scene and left two cardboard narcomensaje . One, signed by the CJNG, read: “This is what will happen to all the lawyers who handle cases for La Familia Michoacana.” Vera has rejected the claim that he represented any members of organized crime groups; evidence suggests the target was the entire newsroom.

Armando Linares, the news director of Monitor Michoacán, stated publicly that the outlet had been receiving escalating threats as a result of its sustained reporting on corruption in local government. “We are not armed, we don’t carry weapons; our only defense is a pen, a pencil, and a notebook,” he said while announcing Toledo’s murder. These threats were reported to local authorities, and the team contacted the Attorney General’s Office to alert them to the risk they faced, but their concerns were not taken seriously.

In the immediate aftermath of the murder, a concerted effort emerged at the municipal and federal levels to deny that Toledo was a journalist. The mayor of Zitácuaro—whom Monitor Michoacán had investigated—claimed Toledo was not registered in the local journalism registrar. Jesús Ramírez Cuevas, AMLO’s spokesman, initially condemned “the murder of journalist Roberto Toledo” on Twitter. However, that same evening, he Tweeted a revised statement: “According to judicial investigations, Roberto Toledo, the citizen murdered today, worked as an assistant at a law firm, not as a journalist.” Ricardo Sánchez Pérez del Pozo, the special prosecutor for the city, told the New York Times that the case fell outside his jurisdiction and that analysis had determined that nothing Toledo had published linked him to the circumstances of the murder. Following Toledo’s murder, Joel Vera — the lawyer financing Monitor Michoacán — and another member of the team went into hiding under federal protection. Armando Linares, the news director, refused to leave Zitácuaro. He was killed forty-three days later.

Heber López Vázquez was the founder and editor of NoticiasWeb and RCP Noticias, based in Salina Cruz, Oaxaca. He was a general assignment journalist who, at the time of his death, was covering political issues and the federal megaproject known as the Interoceanic Corridor of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec. The day before he was killed, López had published a report accusing local politician Arminda Espinosa Cartas of corruption and mismanagement in the construction of a breakwater in Salinas del Marqués, specifically alleging that she coerced construction workers to vote for her in upcoming elections under threat of dismissal.

On 10 February 2022, two men in a pickup truck arrived at the radio studio that López operated from his home. One of them entered the studio and shot López dead. López’s twelve-year-old son, who was present in the home, managed to hide until the gunmen departed. López had reportedly received threats related to his journalism as early as 2019. His family was offered protection measures following his murder, though it is unclear whether these were taken up. Mexico’s OHCHR office condemned the murder.

Notably, one of the men arrested shortly after the murder was Ricardo Espinosa Cartas, the brother of Arminda Espinosa Cartas—the politician about whom López had published multiple articles alleging corruption, including the report published the day before his death. Ricardo Espinosa Cartas and a co-defendant, Ricardo G. R., were convicted as the perpetrators of the homicide and sentenced to thirty-five and forty years’ imprisonment, respectively. This case represents one of the rare instances in which a direct causal link between the victim’s reporting and the murder was established through prosecution, and in which perpetrators received substantial sentences.

Jorge Luis Camero Zazueta, known as “El Choche,” was the director and reporter for El Informativo, a news outlet in Empalme, Sonora. In September 2021, he assumed the position of private secretary to Mayor Luis Fuentes Aguilar. Two weeks before his murder, Camero requested a leave of absence from that municipal position to return to journalism, following the circulation of a video on social media in which Daniel Palafox Suárez—a former congressman who was kidnapped and killed between 28 January and 4 February 2022—was interrogated by cartel operatives and alleged that Camero was involved in uploading information to media pages that reported on cartel activities.

On 24 February 2022, Camero was shot eight times while working out at a local gym in Empalme. Following his death, the Sonora Attorney General’s Office and the State Security Secretariat publicly declared that, based on their investigation, “freedom of expression does not appear to be a motive. Definitely not. This is related, rather, to drug dealing.”  On February 25, Mayor Fuentes Aguilar, whose office had Camero worked in, condemned the murder, stating it had been portrayed as an attempt to “curtail freedom of expression, when I feel that this is not the case.” ARTICLE 19 challenged this characterization, noting the pattern of authorities rapidly dismissing journalistic motives in the killing of reporters. No arrests have been publicly reported in connection with Camero’s murder.

Juan Carlos Muñiz was a journalist who reported on organized crime for Testigo Minero, writing under the pseudonyms “Rigoberto” and “El TX” to protect his identity. Like many journalists in Mexico, Muñiz also worked as a taxi driver to supplement his income from journalism. ARTICLE 19 observed that his case highlighted the economic precarity of journalism in Mexico, where reporters commonly hold multiple jobs—a reality that facilitates official efforts to rule out journalistic motives for murder when the victim held other employment.

On 4 March 2022, Muñiz was found shot dead in his car — which he used both for reporting assignments and as a taxi — in the Los Olivos neighbourhood of Fresnillo, Zacatecas. The same day, the Zacatecas Attorney General's Office declared that it had opened an investigation into the homicide in accordance with cases of attacks against freedom of expression. On 15 March 2022, the Zacatecas Attorney General’s Office announced the arrest of Emanuel de Jesús “N” as the alleged murderer. However, the journalistic community expressed serious concern that the suspect — who was arrested for two separate crimes — was being scapegoated to provide the appearance of resolution and close the case. No clear evidentiary connection between the detainee and Muñiz’s murder has been publicly established.

Armando Linares was the founder and news director of Monitor Michoacán, the same outlet for which Roberto Toledo, killed on 31 January 2022, had worked. Linares founded the publication on the premise that if Mexico were to escape the cycle of violence consuming it, the press would have to investigate the politicians who enabled and facilitated organized crime. The outlet reported on contract fraud, bribery, and police extortion, and was the only news source in Zitácuaro that systematically scrutinized city hall. Among his principal subjects was the mayor, Juan Antonio Ixtláhuac Orihuela, who twelve years earlier had been arrested by federal agents after his name appeared on the CJNG’s payroll, but whose case collapsed and who subsequently regained his office.

Linares and his team had received direct threats from the CJNG “to stop burning the local government and the prosecutor’s office.” The outlet’s lawyer reported these threats to a federal official, providing a list of nine politicians — including the mayor and the local prosecutor — whom the newsroom believed were behind the threats. According to the New York Times, the federal official “didn’t seem to take the story very seriously, stating that these kinds of threats happened often and that the matter would most likely calm down on its own.” In desperation, the outlet paid approximately $24,000 USD to the CJNG in an attempt to secure the safety of the newsroom. Linares made a public request for  protection in the federal Mechanism after this incident, but it is unclear whether it received a response. After Toledo’s murder, Linares told CPJ that he was receiving direct death threats. He was offered protection and assistance in leaving Zitácuaro, which he refused. There are conflicting accounts of whether Linares ever accepted protective measures; the Associated Press reported that his wife stated he had National Guard protection for one month after Toledo’s murder, and CPJ was told by an official of the federal Mechanism that Linares was in-progress of enrolment at the time of his murder. However, most other outlets report that he denied protective measures altogether. Authorities subsequently cited this refusal to characterize him as not in danger due to his work. SEGOB Undersecretary for Human Rights Alejandro Encinas later stated that Linares’ decision not to enroll in the federal Mechanism was the reason for his death. Federal investigators also sought a court order to wiretap the phones of Linares and the outlet’s lawyer; a judge denied the request, ruling that victims of a crime should not be subjected to such surveillance.

On 15 March 2022, forty-three days after Toledo’s murder, a man was observed on security footage approaching Linares as he walked to his apartment. The two were seen speaking before entering together. Minutes later, the man fled the scene. Linares was found inside, shot eight times. Surveillance footage also showed two lookouts casing the area hours before the killing.

The day after Linares’s death, the lawyer financing Monitor Michoacán shut the outlet down and went into hiding, where he remains. The murders had a devastating chilling effect on independent reporting in the region. At a press conference following Linares’ death, then-mayor and frequent target of Monitor Michoacán reporting Antonio Ixtláhuac warned media outlets and commentators to be very careful with their accusations, saying, “I think there needs to be a lot of care in the expressions of commentators and media outlets, although they are respected, of course, but the municipal government of Zitácuaro cannot allow such flippant expressions either… And I think that sometimes there are intentions to destabilize.” Citing data they collected in 2021, ARTICLE 19 wrote that Linares’ muder and the response of authorities sits in a context where 44.25% of journalists attacked cover corruption and politics.

At Linares’s wake, four unknown men arrived; one approached journalists covering the funeral, waved a pistol, and told them: “If you don’t leave in two minutes, you’ll be sorry.” Carlos Gerardo Sánchez Mendoza, identified as a CJNG member, was arrested in August 2023 for the murder. However, he was released in March 2025 due to “lack of conclusive evidence.” In August 2025, a different individual, Magdiel “N,” was arrested for the murder. In a highly-unusual move, the judge revoked Magdiel’s mandatory pretrial detention order, allowing him to face his trial while free. The special prosecutor who had previously dismissed the Toledo case as outside his jurisdiction made the same determination for Linares’s death. In June 2026, two judges involved in the acquittal of Sánchez Mendoza were suspended for alleged irregularities during the investigation first filed in a complaint in December 2025. The administrative investigation into their activities is ongoing.

Luis Enrique Ramírez Ramos was a veteran journalist with a forty-year career who had contributed to some of Mexico’s leading national newspapers and who covered local political issues in Culiacán, Sinaloa. In a 2015 interview, Ramírez disclosed that he and three friends—all of whom were subsequently murdered—had been privy to sensitive information about former Sinaloa Governor Mario López Valdez and ex-government secretary Gerardo Vargas Landeros. Ramírez stated that the threats he had received originated from the state government. He had gone into hiding in 2011 following these threats, taking temporary refuge in Mexico City.

On 5 May 2022, Ramírez’s body was found wrapped in black plastic sheeting on a dirt road near the El Ranchito ejido in Culiacán. He had been kidnapped after leaving his home in the Los Pinos neighbourhood. CNDH and the Sinaloa State Human Rights Commission condemned the murder. On 21 July 2022, authorities announced the arrest and indictment of Brysia Carolina “F” on charges of obstruction of justice, accused of hiding the mobile phone of her partner, who was alleged to have committed the murder. She was released in January 2023 after a judge declined to prosecute. For months, the Sinaloa State Prosecutor’s Office did not act on outstanding arrest warrants against two principal suspects identified by the initials JEGG and SRVV,.  In December 2023, the suspect identified by the moniker SRVV Samuel Rodolfo Vizcarra Velarde, was arrested for Ramírez’s murder. He was found guilty and sentenced to 19 years in prison, which Ramírez’s family found insufficient for the gravity of the murder, in March 2026. It is unclear if efforts have been made to arrest the suspect JEGG.

Yesenia Mollinedo Falconi was the founder and director of El Veraz, a local news outlet in Cosoleacaque, Veracruz, which she established in 2015. Sheila Johana García was a camera operator for the outlet who had been trained by Mollinedo and issued a press credential only five days before her death, on 4 May 2022. Cosoleacaque is located in the southern border area of Veracruz, near Minatitlán, where thirteen people were killed in a mass shooting in 2019. The threats against Mollinedo began after she published articles critical of the Veracruz State Public Security Secretariat.

On 9 May 2022, armed men shot both journalists at least seven times outside a convenience store at the intersection of Benito Juárez and Francisco I. Madero streets in Cosoleacaque at approximately 4:00 p.m. The victims were about to enter a vehicle when gunmen who appeared to have been lying in wait opened fire. Both women were transported to hospital, where they died of their injuries. García’s death was almost certainly collateral: Mollinedo, the target, was the journalist whose reporting had provoked threats. Prior to her death, Mollinedo had told her mother that she was afraid and had been receiving threats by telephone. She was also aware of suspicious individuals following her habitual routes. On 30 April 2022, approximately nine days before the attack, she was threatened by men who were following her. These threats reportedly began when Yesenia started publishing articles critical of the Veracruz State Public Security Secretariat.

In the chaotic aftermath, the Veracruz prosecutor’s office mistakenly detained a university student and food delivery worker from Xalapa who happened to share the same name as a suspect, Antonio de Jesús “N” (“El Mara”). The wrongfully detained individual was released the same evening, hours after his detention on 17 May 2022, following public protests demanding his release. Subsequently, Armando “N” (“El Trascabo”) was arrested on 6 June 2022, and Víctor Manuel “N” (“El Calaco”) on 8 June 2022. Both were formally charged with the murders. The correct Antonio de Jesús “N” (“El Mara”) was arrested on 28 October 2022 and charged on 4 November 2022 for both murders. It is unclear what stage the investigation is currently in.

Antonio de la Cruz was a reporter for El Expreso in Ciudad Victoria, Tamaulipas, where he had worked for more than two decades. While his beat for the newspaper focused on environmental issues—particularly drought and water shortages—De la Cruz also used his personal social media accounts to call out government officials for corruption, exposing alleged malfeasance by local politicians.

On 29 June 2022, at approximately 9:15 AM., De la Cruz was shot dead outside his home as he sat in his car with his twenty-three-year-old daughter, whom he was taking to work. Two armed men on motorcycles opened fire, killing him with four bullets fired from a .40 caliber weapon for the exclusive use of the Army. His daughter was struck in the head. She was taken to a hospital, where emergency surgery was unsuccessful and she died.

No direct threats against De la Cruz were documented prior to the attack, and he was not enrolled in the journalism protection mechanism. However, on 20 December 2018—nineteen days into the AMLO presidency—a severed human head and hands were left outside the offices of El Expreso, constituting a general threat against the publication.

The federal Attorney General assumed jurisdiction after allegations emerged that municipal authorities may have been involved in the murder. ONU-DU and CNDH condemned the murder. In 2025, FEADLE determined that De la Cruz’s murder was indeed attributable to his journalistic reporting: specifically, that hitmen from organized crime had travelled from Nuevo Laredo to Ciudad Victoria to kill him in retaliation for information he published about a criminal gang in El Expreso. Rafael Santiago Arano Rodríguez, “El Piña,” was first identified as a suspect in November 2022 and has been imprisoned  in a state facility in Nuevo Laredo since 2023 for alleged responsibility in the crime, though the trial has been delayed by defence appeals.

Rubén Haro Madero was the founder of Noticias de la Red, a digital news outlet in Sonora, and also served as a public relations official for the municipal government of Nogales. On 17 July 2022, at approximately 2:00 a.m., assailants in a white Honda pickup truck pulled alongside Haro’s car on a road in the Fundó Legal neighbourhood of Ciudad Obregón and fired five shots at him. Haro survived the attack. Approximately one hour before the shooting, Haro’s news outlet had published two videos of shootings in Ciudad Obregón. Haro told CPJ that he had never previously received threats or been targeted. Sonora’s Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation and referred the case to the FEADLE Sonora office. Following the attack, Haro contacted the federal Protection Mechanism with a view to joining a protection programme, but no further details are publicly available regarding the outcome.

Ernesto Méndez was the editorial director of local news website Tu Voz, and also contributed to Periódico Correo and Zona Franca. While he primarily covered general news, ARTICLE 19 disclosed that he had a history of threats dating back seven years, linked to the administration of the late mayor of San Luis de la Paz, Guanajuato, Timoteo Villa. On 2 August 2022, Méndez was shot and killed along with two other people at a bar that he owned, at approximately 23:00. Two others were injured in the attack. On 11 August 2022, the SSPC reported that the murder was related to the extortion of the family business and announced the arrest of one suspect, Roberto “N,” identified as one of two alleged perpetrators. No further update has been provided.

On 11 August 2022, Allan González, a radio announcer at Switch 105.9 FM, along with three non-editorial colleagues—including Armando Guerrero, the operations manager, as well as Lino Flores and Alejandro Arriaga—were recording a promotional segment with a mobile unit outside a Little Caesar’s pizzeria on Ejército Nacional Avenue in Ciudad Juárez when they were killed by an armed group. The attack occurred during a broader wave of coordinated violence by alleged members of organized crime across the neighbourhood, in which civilians were targeted and businesses were set ablaze. In an interview with ARTICLE 19, anonymous sources confirmed that none of the outlet’s contributors had reported prior threats; González’s programming focused primarily on music. Although the attacks were attributed to the Los Mexicles gang, affiliated with the Sinaloa Cartel, the killing of the radio station employees may have been incidental to the broader campaign of terror. Filming publicly in Ciudad Juárez on a day where 11 people were killed may have made the journalists a target. Six members of Los Mexicles were arrested for their participation in the violent acts. Following the attack, other employees of the radio station received threats related to their coverage of the events.

Fredid Román was a veteran journalist and the founder and editor of La Realidad, a newspaper in Chilpancingo, Guerrero, which he closed in 2022 due to financial difficulties from the COVID-19 pandemic. He subsequently became a columnist for Vértice de Chilpancingo and La Realidad de Guerrero. In his final published column, posted on Facebook less than an hour before his execution and titled “State Crime without Blaming the Boss,” Román wrote about the Ayotzinapa case and criticized President AMLO for “exonerating” his predecessor Enrique Peña Nieto of responsibility.

In a finding of significant relevance to this report, investigative reporting by Lighthouse Reports and Haaretz revealed that, on 21 August 2022—the day before Román’s murder—his phone was targeted using telecommunications surveillance infrastructure. Confidential network data showed that a global title leased by a Swiss surveillance broker was used to attempt to extract location data and other information from Román’s device, a technique consistent with SS7 network exploitation. While the precise individual who issued the surveillance command remains unknown, the use of sophisticated telecommunications interception capabilities against a journalist—on the eve of his assassination—raises grave concerns about the involvement of state or state-adjacent actors.

On 22 August 2022, at approximately 4:30 p.m., two men on a motorcycle approached Román as he got into his car outside his home and shot him dead. His death came just one month after his son, Bladimir Román, was shot and killed in Ocotito. During the funeral procession, Román’s relatives revealed that they had received death threats from alleged members of organized crime. On the same day as Román’s funeral, more than fifty journalists protested against impunity for the killing of Román and other Mexican journalists outside the Attorney General’s Office in Mexico City.

The Guerrero Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation examining whether Román’s journalistic work motivated the murder and whether it was connected to his son’s killing. Investigative lines have included a turf war between rival criminal factions over the poultry distribution industry in Chilpancingo, specifically between the Citizen Police of El Ocotito (the armed wing of Los Ardillos, led by José David Barrientos Salazar “El Deivid”) and Los Jaleacos. Barrientos has publicly accused the Román family of having ties to the CJNG and has claimed that allegations linking him to the journalist’s murder are part of a strategy by a rival cartel. In February 2023, José “N,” alias “El Deibi,” was arrested for Román’s murder. “El Deibi” is reportedly the head of a community policing organization affiliated with the armed wing of the criminal group “Los Ardillos.” He was formally charged with Román’s murder in April 2023; no public updates on the case have been shared since.

Roberto Carlos Flores Mendoza, aged 41, was the founder and director of Chiapas Denuncia YA, a Facebook-based news outlet he created in October 2018 covering local and state politics, public security, and citizen complaints of alleged official corruption and abuse in the Comitán de Domínguez region of Chiapas. By 2022 the page had roughly 66,000 followers and published citizens' reports about crime, security, and alleged government corruption. Before turning to journalism, Flores Mendoza had worked for the Comitán de Domínguez municipal government.

On the morning of 20 September 2022, at approximately 11:30 a.m., Flores Mendoza was last seen in the city of Comitán de Domínguez, in the La Pileta neighborhood, according to the missing-person report his wife filed with the FGE of Chiapas. The FGE opened an investigation, and state authorities notified the federal Comisión Nacional de Búsqueda on 21 September. Relatives told local media that he had been intercepted by men traveling in a pickup truck while driving his own vehicle; the official FGE bulletin records only that he was last seen by his wife and does not characterize the disappearance as an abduction. A spokesperson for the FGE told CPJ that authorities had not yet determined whether Flores was abducted, and as of the following week authorities had not established whether the case was connected to his journalistic work.

Around the time of his disappearance, Chiapas Denuncia YA had posted a report about criminal gangs in the area, which was removed shortly afterward; multiple outlets reported that the deleted post concerned an alleged internal dispute within the Sinaloa Cartel in Chiapas. ARTICLE 19 documented the case and reported, based on testimony it gathered, that Flores had indicated he was the target of intimidating messages and that his final post, addressing organized crime, was removed on 19 September. ARTICLE 19 urged the Chiapas government and the federal Secretaría de Gobernación to coordinate with the Comisión Nacional de Búsqueda under the Protocolo Homologado para la Búsqueda de Personas, and CPJ called on Mexican authorities to undertake a credible and exhaustive investigation, noting that 2022 was the deadliest year on record for the country's press.

Ciro Gómez Leyva was one of Mexico’s most prominent broadcast journalists, serving as the presenter of Imagen Televisión’s nightly national news programme and host of the radio show Por la Mañana. His high-profile position made him a frequent subject of public commentary, including by AMLO himself.

In 2021, AMLO introduced a weekly segment to his morning press conference, “Who’s Who in Lies,” which was used to publicly single out and discredit journalists and media figures. In the segment broadcast on 14 December 2022, two days before Gómez Leyva’s assassination attempt, the President targeted him and two other journalists, stating that “if you listen to them too much, you might even develop a brain tumour.” AMLO had previously criticized Gómez Leyva publicly on numerous occasions, suggesting that the journalist was overpaid.

On the evening of 15 December 2022, Gómez Leyva was driving through Coyoacán Avenue in southern Mexico City when a motorcycle carrying two individuals approached his vehicle. One of the riders turned, drew a firearm, pointed it at the journalist’s head, and opened fire. Gómez Leyva survived solely because the vehicle’s armoured plating and bulletproof windows stopped the rounds. The armoured car had been provided to him by his network for the short nightly journey between the studio and his house, following earlier threats related to his reporting on Mexico’s northern prisons.

Mexico City Public Security Minister Omar García Harfuch held a press conference in which he shared security camera footage and preliminary details about the attackers. In January 2023, 16 people were arrested in connection to the attempted murder. In October 2024, Gómez Leyva retired from his television programme and relocated to Madrid, Spain, from where he continues to host his radio show. In June 2025, Pool Pedro Gómez Jaramillo, alias “El Pool,” and Héctor Eduardo Martínez Jiménez, alias “El Bart,” pled guilty to attempted murder and criminal association, receiving sentences of 12 and 14 years in prison respectively. Armando Escárcega, alias “El Patrón,” considered the mastermind of the attack, was arrested in October 2024 in California. He was sentenced to 14 years in prison.

Alan García Aguilar was the founder of Escenario Calentano, a Facebook-based news page covering the Tierra Caliente region of Guerrero. In the months leading up to his disappearance, the page had published extensive coverage of the activities of La Familia Michoacana, a criminal organization operating in the region.

On 27 December 2022, García Aguilar was kidnapped, along with fellow journalist Jesús Pintor Alegre and website administrator Fernando Moreno. The three were abducted separately but held together. A fourth individual, José Alberto Benítez Santos, a municipal employee, was kidnapped separately after being mistaken for one of the page’s administrators. Pintor Alegre later recounted being questioned, beaten, and accused of being the administrator of Escenario Calentano. A video was posted by the perpetrators on the Escenario Calentano Facebook page itself, showing two of the captives, García Aguilar and Moreno, chained hand and foot, with García Aguilar stating: “Escenario Calentano was created five years ago; I was the one who founded the page.” The captors’ accompanying message allegedly read: “So you can see that sooner or later we’ll catch the assholes.”

On 10 and 11 January 2023, the Guerrero State Attorney General’s office issued two statements that they were investigating the kidnapping. Pintor Alegre and Moreno were released on 11 January 2023. Benítez Santos was released on 22 January 2023. Alan García Aguilar remains forcibly disappeared. Multiple sources attribute responsibility to La Familia Michoacana. No prosecutions have been reported, and no legal follow-up on the cases of the surviving victims has been publicly disclosed.

Marco Aurelio Ramírez Hernández was a veteran journalist based in Tehuacán, Puebla. He was a crime reporter for the news programme Cuarto Poder and hosted a programme on Estéreo Luz FM in which he analyzed aspects of public life in the state of Puebla, including human rights violations and alleged irregularities in the exercise of public office. His reporting was notably critical: he had previously covered allegations against the priest Nicolás Aguilar, accused of abusing more than 80 minors. Ramírez Hernández had also served as the Director of Public Safety and Government for the Tehuacán City Council for nine months in 2019, during which time he contributed to the dismantling of a criminal organisation involved in fuel smuggling, drug trafficking, and human trafficking. During that tenure, members of the “Bigotonas” criminal gang were apprehended, which investigators allegedly identified later as a potential motive for his assassination.

On 23 May 2023, at approximately 1:45 p.m., Ramírez Hernández was leaving a residence and boarding his vehicle in the Fraccionamiento Agua Blanca in Tehuacán when two armed men approached and opened fire, striking him at least five times. His vehicle subsequently struck a tree. Ramírez Hernández died at the scene. ARTICLE 19 reportedly requested protective measures for his family following the killing, as did CNDH, though it is unclear whether such measures were ever implemented.

The assassination drew immediate and widespread condemnation from international bodies. The OHCHR in Mexico called upon the authorities to redouble efforts for a prompt and effective investigation and to include the victim’s journalistic work as a line of inquiry. The UNESCO Director-General condemned the killing and urged accountability. RSF demanded an exhaustive investigation. On 26 May 2023, CNDH announced it would monitor the state of Puebla’s investigation into Ramírez Hernández’s killing.

On 31 May 2023, José Francisco N. was arrested for drug trafficking, and was charged on 12 July for aggravated homicide in the murder of Ramírez Hernández. In September 2024, Jesús Armando N., alias “El Güero” was arrested by the Attorney General's Office of the State of Puebla and the State Public Security Secretariat for the murder of Ramírez Hernández. After nearly three years of legal proceedings comprising 24 hearings and the presentation of 50 items of evidence, on 16 February 2026, the Tribunal de Enjuiciamiento of the Judicial Branch of Puebla found Jesús Armando N. and José Francisco N. guilty of aggravated intentional homicide. The court determined that the killing was directly related to the victim’s journalistic activity, specifically his investigation into criminal gangs operating in the Tehuacán region. On 26 February 2026, both were sentenced to 46 years and five months of imprisonment. A third implicated individual remains a fugitive, and the intellectual authors of the crime have not been identified.

Juan Carlos Hinojosa Viveros was a photographer employed in the social communication department of the Nanchital City Council in Veracruz and served as editor of the digital outlet La de 8 News. In the period prior to his disappearance, Hinojosa Viveros was covering migration issues and fires in an industrial zone near the Pemex refinery complex.

On the morning of 6 July 2023, Hinojosa Viveros was last seen in the Factoría area of Nanchital, in the vicinity of the Pemex complex. He was allegedly intercepted by unknown individuals who abducted him in a white van.

As of the date of this report, no substantive updates on the investigation into his disappearance have been made public. Reporting indicates that the journalist’s family has sought to halt any advocacy or additional investigation not completed by the Veracruz Attorney General’s Office; they have not spoken with any media. They successfully lobbied the Veracruz State Commission for the Attention and Protection of Journalists to stop collaborating with the FGE. This raises the troubling possibility that they have been subjected to threats or intimidation by those responsible for the disappearance. Hinojosa Viveros remains one of Mexico’s disappeared journalists, and his case exemplifies the particular dangers faced by reporters covering sensitive topics in regions where criminal organizations exercise de facto control.

Luis Martín Sánchez Íñiguez, aged 59, was a journalist who served as a correspondent for the national newspaper La Jornada and a contributor to the digital outlet criticadn.mx, both based in Tepic, Nayarit. He was a seasoned crime and public security reporter in one of Mexico’s most violent regions.

Three days prior to his disappearance, Sánchez Íñiguez published an article relaying information from the state prosecutor’s office concerning the recovery of eight bodies from a clandestine grave known as “Devil’s Cave,” situated on the northern slope of San Juan Hill, between the limits of Tepic and the municipality of Xalisco. This article attracted significant public attention and may have constituted the trigger for his abduction.

Sánchez Íñiguez’s wife, Cecilia López, last spoke to him on the evening of 5 July 2023 after he returned alone to the family residence in Tepic following a visit to a nearby town. The next day, when he ceased answering his mobile phone, López’s son went to the residence and discovered that his father was gone, along with his laptop computer, mobile phone, and his La Jornada press credential. La Jornada subsequently reported that Sánchez Íñiguez’s computer and digital storage devices had been taken from his home, suggesting the perpetrators sought to seize evidence of his investigative work.

On 8 July 2023, Sánchez Íñiguez’s body was discovered in the village of El Ahuacate near Tepic, bearing clear signs of torture. His body was found bound, with a message affixed to his chest by means of an ice pick, reading: “You can write whatever you want, but don’t mess with the family.” Authorities estimated that the body had been at the site for 24 to 48 hours before discovery.

The Nayarit State Attorney General’s office published a statement acknowledging that Sánchez Íñiguez’s work as a journalist was a significant motive for his killing. By 14 July, FEADLE assumed jurisdiction over the case. Notwithstanding, a climate of secrecy surrounded the investigation, with limited information released to the public or to the victim’s family. In May 2025, Juseff Farid “N” was arrested for and charged with Sánchez Íñiguez’s murder. The district judge alleged that Farid “N” participated in the kidnapping and murder of the journalist along with two others. No other updates on the case have since been made public. The method of killing—abduction, torture, and the display of a threatening message—bears the hallmarks of organized crime reprisal against journalists whose reporting threatens criminal interests.

Nelson Matus Peña was the founder and director of the online news outlet Lo Real de Guerrero, a platform that focused extensively on coverage of violence and criminal activity in Acapulco, Guerrero. Before entering journalism, Matus had served as a member of the Acapulco Fire Department, through which he developed close relationships with members of the security forces, including police and the Red Cross. He became deeply trusted within his community and, owing to these relationships, at times received information about criminal incidents before law enforcement agencies, making Lo Real de Guerrero a leading real-time source of information on crime in the Acapulco region.

Matus had survived at least two prior assassination attempts. In 2017, he survived an armed attack. In 2019, individuals opened fire on him while he was driving his vehicle; on that occasion he escaped unharmed. In the days immediately preceding his death, his outlet published several stories without bylines covering violent incidents and deadly shootouts in Acapulco, consistent with an environment in which the journalists were aware of the personal risks their reporting entailed.

On 15 July 2023, at approximately 3:00 p.m., Matus was shot twice—including once in the head—while standing outside his vehicle in the parking lot of a Coppel department store in the Emiliano Zapata neighbourhood on Vicente Guerrero Avenue in Acapulco. He was found beside the driver’s side door and died from the gunshot wound to his head. Some reporting indicates that Matus was alive when he was found, and died en-route to the hospital.

Authorities in Guerrero sought to distance the killing from Matus’s journalistic work. Officials circulated suggestions that the speed with which Matus arrived at crime scenes indicated he was being tipped off by criminals as early as 2017, and that a rumour was disseminated that the journalist was acting as a spokesman for a cartel. Press freedom organizations identified this as characteristic of the criminalization of journalists by authorities in Mexico at large—whereby officials deflect responsibility by impugning the character of murdered reporters. No arrests have been made in connection with the killing. The case remains unsolved.

Jesús Gutiérrez Vergara, aged 47, was the founder and director of Notiface Prensa Digital, an online news platform based in San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora. He was a known crime reporter who broadcast live police activities on social media and had published material concerning the arrest of an alleged drug trafficker and videos of police vehicles responding to incidents just days before his murder. In the early hours of 25 September 2023, Gutiérrez Vergara was outside his home in the Colonia Aviación neighbourhood, speaking with four off-duty municipal police officers, one of whom was his neighbour. A vehicle carrying armed men arrived and opened fire . The attack killed Gutiérrez Vergara and one police officer and wounded three other officers.

Officials characterized Gutiérrez Vergara as collateral damage in an attack directed at the police officers rather than at the journalist himself. RSF and ARTICLE 19 publicly challenged this characterization and called upon investigators to consider his journalistic work as a line of inquiry. The UNESCO Director-General condemned the killing, as did Mexico’s OHCHR branch. The National Press Club issued a statement demanding that the perpetrators be brought to justice. Following the killing, Gutiérrez Vergara’s family was enrolled in the federal Protection Mechanism.

On 25 October 2024, approximately one year after the journalist’s murder, members of SEDENA forced their way into the family home in the same Colonia Aviación neighbourhood. According to family accounts and security footage, soldiers stopped the children as they were closing their gate, forcibly entered the residence and pulled them outside, pushed them to the ground at gunpoint, and detained them. One of the sons, Caleth Jesús Gutiérrez—who had himself become a journalist—activated his panic button. The soldiers withdrew only after a family member informed them the household was under the protection of the Mechanism. This incident constitutes a grave failure of the Mechanism and suggests that state security forces either disregarded or were unaware of the protection measures in place—or, more troublingly, that the family was deliberately targeted. No progress on the investigation into Gutiérrez Vergara’s killing has been reported as of the date of this report.

Ismael Villagómez Tapia, known as “El Tiger”, was a photojournalist who had worked for El Heraldo de Juárez for approximately 18 years, covering general assignment stories in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, including migration, the migrant caravans, and local crime. His final journalistic assignment was coverage of casualties resulting from a trailer crash at a food stall area. To supplement his income as a journalist, Villagómez Tapia also worked as a driver for InDrive, a ride-hailing application.

In the early hours of 16 November 2023, Villagómez Tapia was found dead from a gunshot wound to the head while seated in the driver’s seat of his grey Hyundai Elantra in the Colonia Fronteriza Alta neighbourhood of Ciudad Juárez. He had been shot at close range with a 9mm weapon. His mobile phone was missing from the vehicle. It was presumed he was working as a ride-hailing driver at the time; passenger records from the InDrive platform contributed to the investigation.

Authorities initially arrested three suspects. Jesús Adrián CL (“El Monky”) and Carlos Miguel HH were apprehended in the hours following the killing and found in possession of two mobile phones belonging to Villagómez Tapia. A third suspect, Johan CB, was detained on federal firearms charges. The Chihuahua state prosecutor characterized the killing as likely connected to a robbery rather than to Villagómez Tapia’s journalism, though he stated the journalistic motive was not ruled out.

The trial began on 13 November 2024. On 28 November 2024, a three-judge tribunal of the Chihuahua Judicial Branch unanimously acquitted CL and HH, finding that the prosecution had failed to present sufficient evidence of their participation in the homicide. The presiding judge identified multiple inconsistencies in the investigation, including the handling of key ballistic evidence: the shell casing from the bullet that killed Villagómez Tapia was not discovered until nine hours after the crime, when the vehicle was already in the prosecutor’s compound, and forensic analysts had failed to conduct swabs of the rear door handles to determine whether anyone had been in the back seat at the time of the shooting. Villagómez Tapia’s widow told El Heraldo de Juárez she was deeply hurt and outraged by the verdict, stating that her husband’s killers had spent only a year in prison. The Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office announced it would appeal. According to the latest reporting on 30 November 2024, The third defendant, Johan CB, remains incarcerated at the Cereso No. 3 state prison on federal firearms charges. The Asociación de Periodistas de Ciudad Juárez condemned the acquittal, stating that someone in the prosecutorial chain had failed to do their job. The case exemplifies the systemic investigative failures that underpin impunity for crimes against journalists in Mexico.

On 28 November 2023, five journalists were shot in two separate but contemporaneous attacks in the Mexican states of Michoacán and Guerrero, an event that drew international attention and underscored the scale of violence against the press.

Maynor Ramón Ramírez (“El May”) was a reporter for ABC de Michoacán based in Apatzingán, Michoacán, specialising in crime and security reporting. At approximately 8:30 p.m., Ramírez was standing outside a carpet cleaning business he owned in the Lázaro Cárdenas neighbourhood, near the “El Ahuate” market, when he was attacked with gunfire. He sustained multiple gunshot wounds to his abdomen and was transferred by Civil Protection paramedics to the emergency area of the regional hospital of the Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (Mexican Social Security Institute, “IMSS”). A 38-year-old employee of the business, identified only as Juan Manuel, was also injured in the attack. Ramírez survived.

This was the second attempt on Ramírez’s life. On 11 October 2016, he had been shot while at the intersection of Lázaro Cárdenas and Francisco I. Madero avenues in Apatzingán. Reports conflict on whether he was shot in the head or stomach. He recovered from the attack, and continued his journalistic work. The Attorney General’s Office of the State of Michoacán initiated an investigation file. No further information has been made public regarding the status of the investigation or any suspects.

The Chilpancingo Attack. On the same date, four photojournalists in Chilpancingo, Guerrero, came under fire while returning together from covering the murder of a bus driver that had taken place that morning. The attack occurred in the vicinity of a military barracks. The victims were: Víctor Mateo Francisco, a photojournalist and contributor to ANG, AHORA Guerrero, and Quadratín, who was shot in the face and sustained grave injuries; Jesús de la Cruz, a photojournalist for Noticias Reportes Guerrero, who was shot in the cervical spine, sustaining life-threatening injuries; Óscar Guerrero, a photojournalist for Amapola Periodismo, who suffered a minor injury to his arm from gunfire; and Héctor Camacho, a photojournalist for Interacción Weekly, who escaped physical harm but whose name was frequently withheld from reporting due to safety concerns.

According to RSF, all four journalists targeted in the Chilpancingo shooting primarily covered crime stories—the “nota roja” or “policíaca” beat—in one of Mexico’s most violent states. The Attorney General’s Office stated that a joint operation involving state and local police, the National Guard, and the Army had been initiated to locate the assailant. No subsequent updates have been made public, and no arrests have been reported.

The Inter American Press Association condemned the attacks. The fact that five journalists were shot on a single day—in two different states but under strikingly parallel circumstances of crime reporters coming under attack—illustrates both the extraordinary danger confronting members of the press who cover organised crime and public security, and the failure of the Mexican state to provide effective protection. The attacks of 28 November 2023 came just days after three other journalists had been abducted and held for days in Taxco, Guerrero, before being released without explanation.

Roberto Carlos Figueroa Bustos, aged 40, was the founder and editor of Acá en el Show, a digital news outlet based in Cuernavaca, Morelos, that published on Facebook and commanded a following of more than 10,000 users. A trained biologist and former state government official, Figueroa transitioned to journalism and online content creation following the 2018 state and federal elections, according to his colleague and friend, the Morelos-based journalist José Montes. Through Acá en el Show, Figueroa published news articles, commentary on local politics, and satirical videos critical of local politicians, including Governor Cuauhtémoc Blanco Bravo of Morelos. On the day of his abduction and killing, Figueroa posted a short video announcing that he possessed information on corruption involving candidates for the upcoming 2 June state and federal elections. He had also recently published a report on the murder of a relative of a candidate for the municipal elections in Tetecala, Morelos. The day before his murder, on 25 April, he participated in an event organised by the centre-left political party Movimiento Ciudadano.

On the morning of 26 April 2024, armed gunmen abducted Figueroa shortly after he dropped off his two daughters at their school in Cuernavaca, approximately 50 miles south of Mexico City. His unidentified captors contacted his wife, Esmeralda, on at least three occasions and demanded a ransom in exchange for his release. During one such call, at approximately 8:00 a.m., Figueroa was put on the telephone and told his wife he needed payment, stating that “it was fine.” In the background, individuals were heard shouting that they would kill her if she called the police. His wife delivered an undisclosed sum at the agreed location near the borders of Cuernavaca, close to the city of Ocuilan. Despite payment of the ransom, after receipt of an anonymous telephone call, Figueroa’s body was discovered later that evening inside a white Ford Ikon on a dirt road in Coajomulco, north of Cuernavaca. He had suffered a fatal gunshot wound to the head. The body of a second, unidentified man was found outside the vehicle.

Figueroa was not enrolled in the federal Mechanism at the time of his killing. An official of the Mechanism told CPJ on 26 April 2024 that the office had no prior knowledge of any threats against Figueroa. His colleague Montes similarly told CPJ that he was unaware of any specific threats against Figueroa’s life and that the journalist did not appear unusually worried in the days preceding his death. However, Montes noted that the Acá en el Show office had been broken into twice — in November and December 2023 — although nothing was reported stolen.

The Morelos state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation. On 29 April 2024, the state attorney general announced at a press conference that Figueroa’s death was “possibly linked to his work as a reporter,” but provided no further details. No arrests have been publicly reported. The killing was condemned by the IACHR Special Rapporteur for Freedom of Expression, the UNESCO Director-General, and ARTICLE 19. RSF joined a special commission of journalists and press freedom defenders assisting the Morelos state prosecutor’s office in investigating the murder. As of the date of this report, no person has been charged or convicted in connection with Figueroa’s killing.

Martín Antonio Olivier Rodríguez was a radio broadcaster and announcer for the radio station La que más suena in Ajalpan, Puebla. He was reported missing by his relatives on the night of 6 May 2024 after he stopped responding to messages following a local council meeting in the Guadalupe Pantzingo neighborhood. His body was found the following day, abandoned in a taxi cab, exhibiting signs of violence. The circumstances of his abduction and the precise cause of death have not been publicly detailed by the authorities. Olivier Rodríguez’s vehicle had been stolen (a completed carjacking) a few days before his murder, though he had recovered it. The IACHR Special Rapporteur for Freedom of Expression condemned Olivier Rodríguez’s murder and called on the competent Mexican authorities to conduct a diligent investigation to clarify the facts and identify those responsible. As of the date of this report, no person has been publicly reported as charged or convicted in connection with Olivier Rodríguez’s killing.

Alberto Amaro Jordán, aged 35, is the founder and editor of La Prensa de Tlaxcala, a digital news outlet based in the state of Tlaxcala, east of Mexico City. He is a third-generation journalist, having followed in the footsteps of his father and grandfather. Since founding the outlet in 2018, Amaro has specialised in reporting on local politics, crime, and corruption. Tlaxcala is recognised as a major hub for human trafficking and sexual slavery, home to powerful, family-run criminal networks that traffic girls and young women across Mexico and the U.S.

On 20 May 2024, at approximately 7:00 p.m., unidentified men driving a red truck passed by Amaro’s residence in Apizaco, Tlaxcala, and yelled death threats at the reporter’s bodyguards stationed at the front gate, declaring that they were going to “kill us all.” Amaro told CPJ that he believed the threats were possibly related to a reporting trip he had taken five days earlier, on 15 May, to the nearby municipality of Ocotlán, accompanied by human rights activist Viridiana Baena Leyva, a member of Madres Buscadoras (Searching Mothers), a national network that searches for missing family members and demands the Mexican federal government address the crisis of nearly 100,000 forced disappearances. Amaro and Baena had travelled to Ocotlán to investigate rumours of clandestine graves. Upon arrival, they were observed by several individuals in the area, and when they departed, a state police vehicle followed them for more than 10 miles.

The May 2024 threats were part of a sustained and well-documented pattern of violence and intimidation against Amaro dating to 2019. According to his interviews with Amnesty International and CPJ, Amaro has been subjected to a campaign of harassment including physical surveillance of himself, his wife, and his children; hacking of his website; and defamatory posts on Facebook accusing him of criminal activity. On multiple occasions, aggressors attempted to force him off the road while driving. A gunman on a motorbike fired shots at him. Intruders attempted to break into his home and fired shots at his property. One of his pet dogs was fatally poisoned. On 15 April 2020, officers of the Tetla police force allegedly threatened and harassed Amaro while he was reporting on a farmers’ protest, with a commanding officer allegedly telling him, “We are going to kill you.” In 2021, the mayor of Tetla de la Solidaridad Eleazar Molina Pérez tried to run Amaro off the highway by attempting to ram into his car; no charges were filed against the mayor. In late 2023, three men claiming to be members of the Sinaloa cartel approached Amaro and offered him money to suppress stories about corrupt police officers and to publish defamatory content targeting those who refused the cartel’s demands. Amaro declined. In January 2024, Amaro was chased by an unknown individual in a vehicle who attempted to ram his car; the Mechanism bodyguard driving managed to evade the attacker. In November 2021, Amaro was arrested for filming state police officers extorting citizens. He further reported that Alfredo “N,” the former Secretary of Public Security of Tlaxcala — who is currently a fugitive facing charges of enforced disappearance—ordered state police to photograph Amaro’s family and track his movements.

Amaro’s case constitutes one of the most extensively documented failures of the federal Mechanism. He enrolled in the Mechanism in 2019 but told Amnesty International and CPJ that it took “months” for the Mechanism to respond to his initial requests for help. Even after enrolment, it took approximately six months for the Mechanism to provide him with a panic button, and bodyguards were not assigned until 2021. One of the vehicles the Mechanism provided for his protection detail had faulty brakes, and the private security company tasked with monitoring his panic button frequently failed to respond to requests for help. Amaro reinforced his property’s perimeter and installed an alarm system and 25 security cameras at his own expense.

In late July 2023, the Mechanism reassessed Amaro’s security situation and concluded that he was no longer at risk. Upon reviewing the evaluation, Amaro found it contained numerous errors and made no mention of the recent poisoning of his dog. Moreover, the evaluation stated that Amaro was no longer in danger because one of the three men who had attempted to bribe him had been arrested — ignoring that the other two remained at large. Facing the prospect of losing his bodyguards and being reduced to a panic button and police visits as his sole protective measures, Amaro hired a lawyer and filed an amparo (injunction). A judge ruled in his favour in August 2023, blocking the removal of his four bodyguards, although the long-term status of his protection remained uncertain.

As a result of the constant attacks and the Mechanism’s failure to guarantee his safety, Amaro reported self-censoring and contemplated abandoning journalism altogether. His case was profiled by Amnesty International and CPJ in their March 2024 joint report, “‘No one guarantees my safety’: The urgent need to strengthen Mexico’s federal policies for the protection of journalists.”

CPJ’s telephone calls to the Tlaxcala State Prosecutor’s Office on 21 and 22 May 2024 regarding the latest threats were not answered. A Mechanism official confirmed to CPJ that the agency was aware of the threats and was investigating, describing Amaro’s protection schedule as “one of the strongest.” No arrests in connection with the 20 May 2024 threats have been publicly reported. Amaro was threatened with a firearm by a state police officer in relation to his reporting in June 2024. The officer pulled up beside the car Amaro was traveling in at a railroad stop and pulled a gun on him, saying: “This is the damn journalist who published a story against my brother.” Amaro called local police, who refused to arrest the officer.
